verses.1: Al-Mizan explains that the distant demonstrative tilka (“those”) conveys emphasis and exaltation. The Manifest Book apparently means the recited Qur’an, which is clear in itself, clarifies other things, and contains divine knowledge and truths concerning the origin and return. It is called mubīn (“manifest”), rather than ḥakīm (“wise”) as at the opening of Yunus, because this chapter concerns and explains the story of Jacob’s family. It is also possible that the Manifest Book means the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ).
verses.2:
Al-Mizan holds that “it” refers to the Book, containing divine signs and true knowledge. Its descent as an Arabic Qur’an means that it was expressed as recited words in the Arabic familiar to the Arabs; it is thus made understandable to the Prophet and his people, in accordance with: We have made it an Arabic Qur’an so that you may apply reason, and indeed it is with Us in the Mother Book surely sublime and wise (43:3–4).

The phrase laʿalla-kum taʿqilūn (“so that you may apply reason”) broadens the address beyond the Prophet. God clothed the Book in Arabic, with its linguistic beauty, so that people could understand its signs and secrets. Had it not been conveyed in familiar, clear Arabic, its understanding would have remained confined to the Prophet through the particularity of its revelation and instruction.

The commentary therefore concludes that the Qur’an’s exact revealed Arabic wording discloses secrets of its verses and realities of knowledge. If its meanings had instead been revealed in the Prophet’s own wording, as sacred narrations are, or translated into another language, some clear secrets would have been hidden from people’s understanding. This divine concern for clear language is confirmed by the Book’s division into definitive verses, which are its foundation, and metaphorical verses (3:7), and by its designation as “a clear Arabic language” in answer to the claim that a non-Arabic-speaking human instructed the Prophet (16:103).
verses.3:
Al-Mizan cites al-Rāghib’s explanation that qaṣaṣ originally means tracing or following a track and hence denotes consecutive accounts or narratives. Thus qiṣṣa means a story, and aḥsan al-qaṣaṣ means the best narrative or account; qiṣaṣ may also be taken as a verbal noun meaning retribution (iqtiṣāṣ).

If qiṣaṣ is a noun, Joseph’s story is the best of narratives because it portrays sincere monotheism in worship and God’s guardianship of His servant: God nurtures him, leads him on the path of love, raises him from humiliation to honor, and brings him from the well, slavery, and the prison of retribution and revenge to glory and kingship. If it is a verbal noun, God’s recounting of the story is the best recounting because it tells a tale of love and passion with utmost chastity and subtlety. The verse thus means that God recounts this best tale through the revelation of the Qur’an, whereas the Prophet had previously been unaware of it.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says Jacob is called “father,” rather than named, to evoke the tenderness and mercy between him and Joseph. “I saw” denotes a dream or trance with dulled external senses, and its repetition stresses that the eleven planets, sun, and moon prostrated collectively before Joseph. The celestial bodies were perceived visually, but their reverence spiritually; the rational masculine plural marks their prostration as knowing and free. The vision prophesied Joseph’s wilāya, distinction, wisdom, dream interpretation, and completed grace, inaugurating God’s nurturing of him. Its enduring promise recalled divine care through every adversity, grounding his patience and reliance, as God gives His chosen ones glad tidings of their coming blessings and closeness.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that kayd means a stratagem or scheme: it may be praiseworthy or blameworthy, though it is more commonly used negatively, and it may be transitive or intransitive.

Jacob understood Joseph’s vision with certainty as a sign that God would care for him, elevate him, and distinguish him among Jacob’s descendants. Since the dream portrayed Joseph’s brothers, together with Jacob and his wife, bowing to Joseph, Jacob feared that the brothers’ pride and envy would lead them to plot to prevent its fulfilment. Calling him “My son” (bunayya), Jacob tenderly warned Joseph not to reveal the dream before explaining its meaning or the divine honour awaiting him. The warning shows both Jacob’s deep concern for Joseph and his awareness of his other sons’ jealousy and hostility.

The wording directly connects recounting the dream with the brothers’ likely scheme. Their jealousy is the immediate cause, while Satan is a further cause that intensifies it: as man’s manifest enemy, he tempts people away from righteousness and happiness and sows discord among relatives and friends. Thus Jacob’s meaning is apparently that Joseph’s brothers may resent him and, under Satan’s instigation, scheme against him.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s choosing of Joseph, His teaching him the interpretation of dreams, and His completing His blessing upon Joseph and the house of Jacob unfold the meaning of Joseph’s vision.

Ijtibāʾ, “choosing,” derives from a root meaning to gather and preserve from dispersion. When God chooses a servant, He directs mercy toward him, distinguishes him by grace and honour, gathers his affairs, protects him from Satan’s deceptive paths, guides him to the straight path, and makes him exclusively devoted to Himself. Joseph was accordingly among God’s dedicated servants.

Taʾwīl is the realization in external reality of what a vision presents in a form suited to the dreamer’s perceptions. Thus the future prostration of Joseph’s parents and brothers appeared as the prostration of the sun, moon, and eleven planets. Aḥādīth, literally “discourses,” can denote dreams because a dream presents or narrates matters within the self, just as speech presents matters to an audience. Some hold that true dreams arise from an angel’s discourse and false ones from the devil’s; yet dreams can also merely reflect physical conditions, such as heat or cold. The objection that Joseph’s dream and other dreams contain no spoken discourse mistakes “discourse” for verbal speech: dreams symbolically depict events, as words depict them in speech. They may therefore be divine, devilish, or personal internal presentations.

The “discourses” whose taʾwīl Joseph was taught are not confined to dreams. They include occurrences in wakefulness as well as sleep, because such events are connected with their underlying truths and intended outcomes, connections God enables one to perceive. Joseph’s interpretations of dreams, his foretelling in prison, and God’s revelation to him in the well all support this broader sense.

Niʿma is a good, suitable condition, marked by softness, goodness, and fitness; it applies particularly to human beings, who can discern benefit from harm. Wealth, children, rank, and similar gifts are not blessings for a person merely by being possessed. They are blessings only when they conduce to felicity through divine guardianship (wilāya), drawing their recipient near to God. When they lead to misery under Satan’s guardianship, they are curses instead. As attributed to God, gifts are favour, grace, and mercy, for He does not intend evil through His bestowal; but an ungrateful recipient turns them into a curse. Even incomplete means of life are blessings, though completed blessing is the possession of all that is needed for a felicitous life without deficiency.

The completion of blessing in this verse concerns Joseph and the house of Jacob—Jacob, his wife, and all his children—but Joseph is its principal subject and his family is supplementary to him. This accords with the vision, in which the household appeared as the sun, moon, and eleven planets prostrating to him. Joseph’s completed blessing included his special election, knowledge of interpretation, governance, prophethood, kingship, and honour in Egypt. His family’s blessing included Jacob’s consoling reunion with Joseph and the family’s removal from pastoral life in the wilderness to Egypt.

God completed this favour upon Joseph and Jacob’s household as He had earlier completed it for Abraham and Isaac, granting those forefathers the good of this world and the Hereafter. The naming of Abraham and Isaac stresses that the divine favour continues through Abraham’s house by way of Isaac, encompassing Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Jacob’s descendants.

The verse therefore means that, as indicated by the vision, God will choose Joseph for Himself, purifying him from every association with other than God; teach him the realities signified by events seen asleep or awake; and consummate the blessing of divine guardianship through his establishment in Egypt, reunion with his family, sovereignty, and honour. God does so as the One fully knowing His servants’ circumstances and wise in apportioning what they deserve.

Al-Mizan draws several conclusions. First, Jacob too was chosen and taught interpretation, since he interpreted Joseph’s vision with certainty rather than conjecture. Joseph’s own statements in prison show that this knowledge belonged to the heritage of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Their exclusive devotion to God and freedom from associating partners with Him was the ground upon which God taught them interpretation; knowledge of interpretation thus results from such sincere devotion.

Second, the prostration in Joseph’s vision, including Jacob’s, cannot have been worship of Joseph. It was prostration before him for God, as one prostrates toward the Kaʿba while worshipping God alone. It signified Joseph’s own exclusive devotion to God. The celestial form of Jacob’s household also signifies their elevation, radiance, and flourishing in a religiously vital life in this world and the Hereafter.

Third, completing blessing for the whole household does not conflict with uniquely choosing Jacob and Joseph or teaching them interpretation. Divine guardianship has degrees, so each may receive a share of blessing while particular ranks belong only to some. A quality may also be attributed to a group when only some members possess its particular components.

Fourth, Joseph was the means through whom God completed His blessing upon Jacob’s household. This explains why Jacob places Joseph first—“upon you and upon the house of Jacob”—repeatedly says “your Lord,” and leaves Abraham and Isaac outside the principal focus. Joseph stands at the forefront of God’s special care and of the completion of blessing for his family.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph’s story contains signs of God’s oneness: God guards His devoted servants, raises them to honour, and governs causes according to His own decree rather than human intention or outward probability. His brothers meant the well and sale into slavery to destroy and humiliate Joseph, but God made those very means his preservation and elevation. Likewise, the shirt by which they deprived Jacob of sight became the means by which his sight was restored.

Thus every apparent route to Joseph’s ruin became a route to his good end, as Joseph himself later ascribes God’s favour to Godwariness, patience, deliverance from prison, and God’s guardianship in this world and the Hereafter. “For the seekers” (li al-sāʾilīn) indicates that people had asked the Prophet about this story or related matters, occasioning the revelation of the sūrah.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿuṣba denotes a closely united, strong group. Here it refers to Joseph’s ten elder brothers, who managed Jacob’s livestock, wealth, and household. By singling out “Joseph and his brother,” they indicate that the two were full brothers through their mother and only paternal half-brothers to the others; narrations name the brother Benjamin. The two were young and did not share the elders’ responsibilities.

The brothers’ claim that Jacob was in “manifest error” (fī ḍalāl mubīn) does not charge him with religious misguidance. They considered his priorities socially unsound: although they were the capable group on whom his livelihood depended, he devoted exceptional attention to two young boys. Their later admissions of sin, requests for forgiveness, acknowledgement that God preferred Joseph, and desire to win Jacob’s exclusive love show that they believed in God, recognized Jacob’s prophethood, and still loved and respected him. Their later accusation that Jacob persisted in error likewise concerns what they regarded as his excessive attachment to Joseph, not religion.

Jacob’s affection was not mere instinctive partiality. As a servant purified for remembrance of the abode, he perceived righteousness and spiritual perfection in Joseph and his brother; Joseph’s dream especially disclosed his future divine election, knowledge of dream-interpretation, and completed favour upon Jacob’s family. Jacob’s protectiveness revealed this special regard and heightened the elders’ envy. The envy already existed before Joseph disclosed the dream, which only intensified it.

The commentary rejects the view that their jealousy arose principally from different mothers, ordinary parental tenderness toward the youngest, or Jacob’s inability to resist emotional inclination. Maternal differences can affect sibling relations, but if that were the decisive cause, they would have treated Joseph’s brother as they treated Joseph. Ordinary care for weak children is normally intelligible to older siblings, whereas Jacob’s honouring and guarding of Joseph exceeded such care. More fundamentally, excusing a prophet’s preference as an irresistible desire would undermine moral discipline, divine commands and prohibitions, and the elevated station of prophets. God describes Jacob and the other prophets as chosen, guided, righteous, and exclusively devoted to Him; they prefer God’s pleasure to desire.

Al-Mizan also rejects the claim that the brothers were prophets who committed only permissible or pre-prophetic minor sins, or were merely excusable adolescents. Such claims are speculation, and (4:163) does not establish their individual prophethood. They were children of prophets who envied and wronged Joseph, then repented; Jacob and Joseph sought God’s forgiveness for them.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan treats this as the second stage of the brothers’ secret plot. Believing that Joseph and his brother had diverted Jacob’s love from them and endangered their own standing, they proposed either killing Joseph or sending him to a land from which he could not return. They ultimately adopted a form of the second proposal: putting him in a well so that a caravan would carry him far away and erase his trace.

Although both Joseph and his brother had been mentioned earlier, Joseph was the immediate target because he was the principal object of Jacob’s attention, was older, and had the dream indicating special divine favour; perhaps the mention of both also reflects Jacob’s affection for their mother. To “cast him away into some land” uses an indefinite land and the verb ṭarḥ, suggesting the disposal of someone regarded as worthless. Removing Joseph was meant to make Jacob’s countenance—that is, his undivided love and attention—belong to them alone.

Their resolve to become righteous afterwards apparently means repentance after killing or exiling him. This shows that they knew the act was sinful, but envy led them to imagine that a deliberately premeditated sin could be cancelled by planned repentance. Al-Mizan rejects this as genuine repentance: one who intends to sin and then repent is continuing the original intention to disobey and evade punishment, not returning remorsefully to God. A reported alternative understands their becoming righteous as the worldly improvement of their affairs with their father after Joseph’s removal.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that al-jubb is an unlined well, unlike a stone-lined biʾr, and that ghayāb is its dark, unseen recess. One brother proposed the non-lethal version of casting Joseph away: placing him in a well on a travellers’ route so that a caravan would draw water, find him, and carry him to a distant land. This retained some compassion, since it did not directly aim at his death, and the brothers’ later conduct shows that they accepted it.

The Qur’an leaves the speaker unnamed. Reports identifying him as Reuben, Judah, or Levi, and debates about the well’s location or whether “the well” denotes a known particular well, add no significant benefit to understanding the narrative.
verses.11: Al-Mizan reads the brothers’ words as showing their unanimous abandonment of murder in favour of putting Joseph in the well. To carry out their plan, they had to overcome Jacob’s reluctance to entrust Joseph to them. Addressing him tenderly as “Father,” they professed goodwill toward Joseph and asked why he did not trust them with him. They then requested that he send Joseph to their grazing grounds, where he could enjoy himself while they supposedly watched over him.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that the brothers proposed a day of grazing, eating fruit, and play, while emphatically pledging to guard Joseph. Their assurances proceed naturally: they first claim enduring goodwill toward him, request to take him the next day, and then promise protection. “We are indeed his well-wishers” denies any intention to harm him, while “we will indeed take care of him” purports to protect him from external danger.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that Jacob does not openly accuse his sons of intending harm. He instead says that Joseph’s departure would grieve him, gently conveying his distress without provoking their defiance. He then gives the reasonable concern that, amid grazing lands where predators may be found, the brothers could become occupied and a wolf could attack the unattended child.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that the brothers answer as though Jacob feared only a wolf, not their own designs. Stressing that they were a hardy group, they imply that Joseph’s being eaten while they were present would prove them utter failures—something they claim cannot happen. Their emphatic assertion was meant to reassure Jacob and carried an implicit promise of vigilance, which they soon contradicted when they later alleged that the wolf had eaten Joseph while they had left him with their things (12:17).
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that ajmaʿū signifies a considered, unanimous convergence of purpose. Having persuaded Jacob to let Joseph go with them, the brothers jointly resolved to put him into the well.

The omitted result after “when they took him away and conspired to put him into the recess of a well …” is a rhetorical silence that magnifies the horror of their treatment of an innocent child, a prophet and son of prophets, by brothers who knew their father’s love for him. It displays the destructive force of envy before the narrative resumes with God’s revelation to Joseph.

The apparent sense of this revelation is prophetic inspiration. “This affair of theirs” is their casting him into the well, and “while they are not aware” may refer to their ignorance of the revelation or, more fully, of the true reality of their deed. They imagined that they had effaced Joseph’s name, light, and worth; in fact, that act would lead to honour, sovereignty, lasting remembrance, and elevation. Joseph would one day disclose this reality to them, as his words, ‘Have you realized what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were senseless?’ … ‘I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Certainly Allah has shown us favor’ (12:88–90), show. Informing people of what they did is, in this reading, a disclosure of the true nature and outcome of their deeds.

Other explanations say that he would tell them of their act while they did not recognize him, that “informing” means punishing them, or that it refers to his future outward domination over them. A view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās connects it to Joseph’s recognition of them in Egypt and a cup that disclosed their former deed. Al-Mizan considers such interpretations, especially those replacing verbal disclosure with mere external manifestation, far-fetched or unsupported by Joseph’s later question. It finds plausible, but unnecessarily restrictive, the interpretation that they were unaware only of the revelation itself.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that ʿishāʾ is the end of the day, said by some to extend from the Maghrib prayer until dusk. The brothers came weeping so that their account would appear true and their father would not doubt them.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that nastabiq means racing or competing with one another, whether on foot or in an activity such as throwing. It rejects Rashīd Riḍā’s attempt to distinguish it sharply from tasābuq: both can convey competitive striving according to context. Thus “so take the lead in all good works” entails striving to surpass others in reward and nearness to God, while “They raced to the door” describes Joseph and the wife of Potiphar each trying to reach it first for opposed ends. The intensified form istibāq conveys earnest exertion to attain success.

Muʾmin in “you will not believe us” means one who confirms their words. The brothers’ account was that they had gone out racing, probably a foot race, left Joseph with their belongings, and a wolf had devoured him. Their claim that Jacob would not believe them even if they spoke truly is the defensive language of deceivers who know their story is unconvincing but use that very difficulty to simulate sincerity.

Their sham blood (dam kadhib) exposed them: kadhib functions hyperbolically, as though the blood itself were lying, and the indefinite bloodstain was weak evidence. An intact shirt was incompatible with the claim that a wolf had eaten Joseph. Al-Mizan generalizes that falsehood cannot endure because reality is an ordered network of inseparable circumstances and consequences. A liar may conceal one fact but cannot suppress all its implications; some accompanying reality will disclose the contradiction. Truth therefore prevails even when falsehood temporarily appears effective, whereas those who treat truth as falsehood construct a conflicting and perplexed system of belief.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains that Jacob recognizes the brothers’ deceit when they return weeping with the blood-stained shirt, knowing both their envy and their insistence on taking Joseph away. By saying, “Rather your souls have made a matter seem decorous to you,” he rejects the wolf story without specifying the matter their souls had prompted, and he chooses not to punish them. Since he could not determine what had become of Joseph or confront his powerful sons, graceful patience was his necessary course.

“Yet patience is graceful” means that he will bear the ordeal because patience is beautiful; its indefinite form heightens either its excellence or the bitterness of practising it. Patience is not passive surrender to harm. It preserves inner balance, sound judgement, and the capacity to withstand adversity, while people who lack it may collapse into confusion and loss of direction.

Yet patience alone is a defensive fortress, not the independent source of restored security and victory. A believer must preserve inward order through patience and then rely on God, who transcends causes and can repel harm and direct events to their best outcome. Jacob accordingly joins patience to “Allah is the resort against what you allege”: he entrusts to God the exposure of their allegation and Joseph’s recovery, rather than relying on outward means without God’s permission.

This is a prayer for God’s exclusive help. By omitting “I will be patient” and “I will seek help,” and mentioning only God, Jacob shows perfected monotheistic reliance: the affair belongs solely to God. Even his grief and love for Joseph are for God and through God.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that a caravan sent its water-drawer (wārida-hum) to the well. He let down his bucket (adlā dalwahu), expecting water, and was therefore surprised to announce the discovery of a boy. The travellers then concealed Joseph as merchandise, intending to sell or trade him.

“And Allah knew best what they were doing” may express condemnation and their accountability for a sinful act, or may indicate that the event occurred by God’s knowledge and arrangement so that Joseph would reach the destiny appointed for him. His extraction, sale, and journey to Egypt became the means of his later honour, sovereignty, and prophethood.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains that thaman bakhs is a price below an item’s value, darāhima maʿdūda is a small number of counted dirhams, and zāhidīn denotes those who have little desire for something or are wary of it. Sharaw here means selling, not buying.

The context indicates that both pronouns—“they sold him” and “they set small store by him”—refer to the caravan that found and concealed Joseph. They sold him cheaply, apparently fearing that his true status as a free person rather than a slave might be discovered and he taken from them. The following mention of the Egyptian buyer confirms that this purchase was made in good faith.

Al-Mizan rejects the majority view that Joseph’s brothers returned, claimed he was their servant, and sold him to the caravan, as well as the mixed reading that makes the brothers sellers and the caravan reluctant purchasers. The preceding pronouns refer to the caravan, and the brothers have not been mentioned again so as to supply their antecedent. Narrations describing the brothers’ sale of Joseph likewise do not accord with the apparent context or with other reports on the subject.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that the caravan brought Joseph to Egypt, where an Egyptian bought him and took him into his household. References later in the story to the buyer as his wife’s sayyid, as the chieftain whose wife solicited her slave boy, and as one who had a prison show that he was an eminent authority. Joseph thus entered a noble house, though the verse initially calls him simply “the man from Egypt” because the narrative then requires no fuller description.

His instruction to his wife to give Joseph an honourable place shows that he recognized unusual promise in the boy and hoped Joseph might benefit them or become their adopted son. Al-Mizan infers that this prominent man, called al-ʿAzīz in the Qur’an and Potiphar in the Bible, discerned Joseph’s exceptional beauty, dignity, patience, eloquence, wisdom, nobility, and lineage from his youth. His wish to adopt Joseph further suggests that he and his wife were childless.

Makkanā, “We established,” can signify settlement in a place, rank, ability, or empowerment. Here it includes Joseph’s security and stability in Egypt after the well, sale, exile from his father, and lodging in Potiphar’s house. God twice states that He established Joseph in the land: first at this stage and later after his release from prison and appointment over Egypt’s treasuries. Both instances display God’s special care.

“Thus We established Joseph in the land” may compare the establishment just described with itself in order to emphasize its abundance, or it may point from this first part of his history to the complete establishment still to come. In either case, the pattern is that God turns the very plots intended to deprive Joseph of comfort and freedom into means of his security and eventual authority: his brothers’ plot leads to settlement in Potiphar’s house, the women’s plot reveals his sincerity, and imprisonment leads to his full establishment in Egypt.

The purpose clause, “that We might teach him the interpretation of dreams,” states one purpose of this establishment; the omitted part of the statement indicates further unstated purposes. Finally, “Allah has command of His affairs” means that all created causes and events are subject to God’s command and carry out His will; none can evade, precede, or act independently of Him. Most people mistake apparent causes for self-sufficient powers and therefore fail to recognize this divine governance.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that bulūgh al-ashadd, “coming of age,” is the period when bodily strength and faculties are fortified and childhood has faded, usually beginning around eighteen and extending to full intellectual maturity. Here it apparently means the beginning of young adulthood, not its midpoint or its completion at forty. In the account of Moses, coming of age is followed separately by becoming fully mature (wa istawā) (28:14), while another verse separately says that one comes of age and reaches forty years (46:15). Thus, views identifying it with thirty, thirty-three, or forty are untenable; it would be implausible for Potiphar’s wife to have waited through Joseph’s youthful prime only to desire him near middle age.

“We gave him judgement” (ḥukm) means that God granted Joseph decisive speech that resolves disputed matters, together with clear understanding of matters concerning the origin and return to God, ethics, divine laws, and social norms. Joseph’s words, “Sovereignty (ḥukm) belongs only to Allah” (12:40), and, “The matter about which you inquire has been decided (quḍiya al-amr)” (12:41), show that this was God’s judgement: Joseph’s decree was God’s decree, akin to the judgement Abraham requested when he said, “My Lord! Grant me judgement, and unite me with the Righteous” (26:83).

“Knowledge” (ʿilm) is knowledge bestowed by God and therefore free of ignorance (jahl), just as this judgement is untouched by personal desire or devilish insinuation. Since Allah carries through His command, the judgement He grants contains neither doubt nor hesitation, and the knowledge He grants contains no ignorance.

These gifts are not arbitrary: the clause “and thus do We reward the virtuous” indicates that they recompensed Joseph’s prior righteousness. Al-Mizan further infers that every benefactor receives, according to the character of his good deeds, a degree of discernment and knowledge suited to his rank in virtue. Joseph’s knowledge must also have included the interpretation of dreams, since the promise to teach him this precedes the verse and he later tells his prison companions that it is among what his Lord taught him (12:37).
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that rāwadat-hu denotes persistent, gentle solicitation intended to change another’s mind, and thus implies that Joseph was resisting her. Al-Rāghib’s explanation is supported by the term’s uses elsewhere in the story, including Joseph’s statement, ‘It was she who solicited me’ (hiya rāwadatnī ʿan nafsī) (12:25), the townswomen’s statement, ‘The chieftain’s wife has solicited her slave boy’ (turāwidu fatā-hā ʿan nafsi-hi) (12:30), her eventual confession, and Joseph’s brothers’ intention to solicit Benjamin from Jacob. Al-Ṭabrisī likewise defines murāwada as a kindly request meant to obtain compliance. Ghallaqat means that she securely locked the doors, with the intensified form emphasizing either their firm locking or the extremity of her act. Hayta la-ka is an imperative, ‘Come!’; maʿādh Allāh means ‘I seek refuge in God,’ with maʿādh standing in place of aʿūdhu.

The verse gives the attempted seduction with great brevity, but its wording and the wider narrative disclose its gravity. Joseph had entered Potiphar’s household as an apparently unknown young Hebrew slave. His lineage and the creed of his fathers became known only later, when he told his prison companions, ‘I follow the creed of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob’ (12:38). His attachment to God was first made manifest in this encounter through: ‘God forbid! Indeed He is my Lord …’ (12:23). Yet he had retained what Jacob taught him concerning monotheism and servitude to God, his dream’s promise of reunion with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the betrayal by his brothers, and God’s promise in the well that he was under divine care and would confront them while they did not recognize him.

Consequently, Joseph saw himself encompassed by God’s subtle blessings and guardianship. This awareness made him patient through adversity, without complaint, despair, or loss of direction; he later expressed the same principle to his brothers: ‘Indeed if one is Godwary and patient Allah does not waste the reward of the virtuous’ (12:90). His heart remained occupied with God’s acts, signs, protection, and lordship. His love for God steadily deepened until nothing distracted him from his Lord, as his later words also show: ‘It is not for us to ascribe any partner to Allah’ (12:38), ‘Sovereignty belongs only to Allah’ (12:40), and You are my guardian in this world and the Hereafter! (12:101). His purity was a devotion reserved wholly for God.

At first, however, only Joseph’s outward dignity, beauty, and nobility were apparent. Potiphar’s instruction, ‘Give him an honorable place. Maybe he will be useful to us, or we may adopt him as a son’, indicates that he perceived in Joseph a special worth. Potiphar’s wife was instructed to treat him honorably and did so with unusual care. Drawn by his beauty and virtues, her affection became overpowering love when he reached maturity. Her noble standing, beauty, pride, determination, authority over a servant she regarded as her possession, and access to the means available to the powerful all intensified her passion and confidence that he would obey.

She continually hoped to obtain Joseph, employing allure and solicitation; Joseph’s patience and silence may have encouraged her. Finally, driven by her passion, she isolated him in her house, locked the doors, and commanded him to come. She relied on her authority, her preparations, and the apparent absence of any obstacle except his compliance. The scene therefore placed a young man absorbed in love for God alone before a woman wholly absorbed in desire for him.

Joseph’s answer was not based on fear of Potiphar, concern for his own reputation, invocation of his lineage, hope for reward, fear of punishment, or even an explicit assertion of his own strength. Had his heart depended on such external considerations, the commentary maintains, he would have mentioned them in so severe a trial. Rather, he said simply, ‘God forbid!’ He did not say, ‘I seek refuge from you in God,’ and thus differed from Mary’s statement to the spirit: ‘I seek the protection of the Allbeneficent from you, should you be Godwary!’ His unqualified appeal to God manifests a monotheism in which his heart was fixed on God alone and even self-regard had disappeared.

‘Indeed He is my Lord; He has given me a good abode. Indeed the wrongdoers are not felicitous’ explains his seeking refuge. The kindness Joseph had received through Potiphar’s household, including the command to give him an honorable place, was in reality a blessing from God, who alone managed his affair and gave him his good abode. To yield would be wrongdoing, and wrongdoing does not bring felicity, guidance, or peace before God. His words thus affirm that God alone is his Lord, rejecting both the notion of multiple lords and the practical association of partners with God through treating apparent causes as independent. Although Potiphar and his wife were outwardly the means of Joseph’s honorable treatment, Joseph saw its true source in God.

The commentary further holds that Joseph’s indirect answer reflects his recognition that he possesses no independent power to benefit or harm himself; he therefore did not say, ‘I will not do as you command,’ ‘I will not commit such a sin,’ or even ‘I seek refuge in God from you.’ His references to himself in ‘He has given me a good abode (aḥsana mathwāya)’ express dependence, humility, and need. By employing iḥsān, he also alludes to the honor in Potiphar’s command, ‘Give him an honorable place (akrimī mathwā-hu)’.

Thus, though outwardly an encounter between Joseph and Potiphar’s wife, the event was in reality a contest between divine love and worldly lust. God’s attraction and love prevailed, for God has command of His affair. The phrase ‘The woman in whose house he was solicited him’ indicates that the setting itself strengthened her temptation, since the house was hers. Her secure locking of the doors underscores the extremity of her intention, while her imperative ‘Come!’ expresses her perceived dominance and her conviction that all was prepared. Yet God was nearer to Joseph than Joseph himself or the woman was.

Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that ‘Indeed He is my Lord; He has given me a good abode’ refers to Potiphar as Joseph’s master, so that Joseph merely refused to betray the man who had treated him well. If that were intended, the fitting conclusion would have been that betrayers do not prosper, as in Joseph’s later statement: ‘that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not further the schemes of the treacherous’ (12:52), rather than that wrongdoers do not prosper. Nor would Joseph call Potiphar ‘my Lord’ (rabb). Although he used rabb for another person’s master when speaking to a prison companion and the king’s messenger, he never called the king or Potiphar his own lord. In asking the messenger about the women who cut their hands, he said, ‘My Lord is indeed well aware of their stratagems,’ distinguishing God as his Lord from the messenger’s lord. This reading is also supported by the following verse’s words: had he not beheld the proof of his Lord (12:24).
verses.24:
Al-Mizan holds that Joseph’s deliverance in this encounter can be understood only by considering the extraordinary force of its temptations. He was young, beautiful, living in comfort and luxury, alone with a beautiful and powerful aristocratic woman who was consumed by desire for him, had treated him generously, locked the doors, and could plausibly conceal the matter or turn any evidence against him. Yielding could appear to promise enduring power, honour, and wealth. Fear of exposure was ineffective in such circumstances, since she could manipulate the accusation, as later happened; noble ancestry was no safeguard, as Joseph’s own brothers showed; and social prohibitions against treachery lose their deterrent power where enforcement is absent, corrupt, or unaware. Nothing could protect him except monotheism, or, equivalently, the divine love that filled his heart and left no room for anything else.

The verse explains this protection. The evil and indecency turned away from Joseph are the seduction and private seclusion to which he was invited. “So it was” refers to his beholding the proof of his Lord: because Joseph was among God’s devoted servants, God showed him that proof and thereby diverted evil and indecency from him. The phrase “had he not beheld the proof of his Lord” restricts the sense of “he would have made for her.” Al-Mizan reads the two initial clauses as conjoined and emphatically sworn statements, while the consequence of the conditional is implicit: she certainly made for him, and had he not seen his Lord’s proof, he too would have made for her and approached sin.

Yet hamm, “to make for,” denotes an intended act accompanied by movement toward it or its preliminaries, and is used where an obstacle prevents completion. Therefore the counterfactual does not mean that Joseph would certainly have committed adultery. Had he not seen the proof, he would have desired her and drawn near to the act, but would not necessarily have completed it. In the context, sūʾ, “evil,” is the desire and inclination toward her, while faḥshāʾ, “indecency,” is the actual vile act, namely adultery. God says that He turned evil and indecency away from Joseph, not that He turned Joseph away from them. This wording means that desire and the act themselves were kept from him; it does not portray him as possessing an inclination requiring restraint. Thus Joseph neither committed adultery nor actually stood on the verge of it, though the counterfactual establishes what might have occurred without the divine proof.

The proof (burhān) is a conclusive evidence that yields certainty and removes doubt. The Qur’an does not specify what Joseph saw, but it must have given him an unclouded certainty unlike ordinary knowledge of benefit and harm, for such ordinary knowledge can coexist with error and sin. Joseph’s later plea, “If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them and become one of the senseless. (12:33),” likewise shows that his knowledge was not merely conventional moral awareness. The proof granted to devoted servants is unveiled knowledge and witnessed certainty: once it takes hold of the soul, it does not incline to sin. “Beholding” (ruʾya) accordingly means either actual sight or a profound spiritual witnessing, not merely intellectual reflection on religious prohibitions.

The lām in “that We might turn away” may be purposive or causative, without changing the result: Joseph was shown the proof in order, or because of God’s will, to turn both sinful inclination and the indecent act away from him. His being one of God’s dedicated servants is the reason for this treatment. Such servants are chosen exclusively for God, obey no satanic misguidance, temptation of the soul, or call away from Him, and are shown His signs so that they neither sin nor contemplate sin. This is the meaning of infallibility (ʿiṣma, or ‘divine protection’): it rests on a certainty grounded in knowledge, but not in the familiar conventional sciences.

Al-Mizan rejects reports that depict Joseph as nearly undressed with the woman, repeatedly unmoved by warnings, and finally stopped only by a spectacular intervention. Reports cited from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, ʿIkrima, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and others portray him as desiring the act until a proof arrived. Al-Ghazālī records variant accounts of that proof: a warning bird; Jacob appearing in distress; the woman covering her idol and Joseph drawing a lesson from it; an inward voice; written warnings; angels; a barrier; a maiden of paradise; the well of Joseph’s childhood; an ugly appearance of the woman; or a threatening snake. Al-Suyūṭī in al-Durr al-manthūr transmits, on the authority of Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, Ibn Jubayr, and others, a report that Jacob struck Joseph’s chest and his desire departed through his fingertips. Al-Zamakhsharī likewise relates accounts in al-Kashshāf of Joseph preparing himself for intercourse and not desisting after repeated admonitions until Jacob or Gabriel intervened.

The commentary considers these accounts incompatible with Joseph’s prophethood, infallibility, and the Qur’anic description of him as a devoted, wise, knowledgeable, patient, righteous, truthful servant, free of treachery, injustice, and ignorance. A man who intended adultery with a married woman who had received him kindly, persisted after repeated divine warnings, and stopped only through terror or a miraculous expulsion of desire would not be fit for prophethood or divine revelation. Such reports are internally inconsistent, derogate from Joseph as similar tales derogate from Abraham, and are described as Judeo-Christian accretions and fabrications.

Nor would even a slight lapse by Joseph have been left unmentioned, since the slips, repentance, and supplications of Adam, David, Noah, Job, and Jonah are reported. Instead, the Qur’an presents Joseph as an enduring model of chastity and steadfastness. His innocence is confirmed by God’s statement that he was among the dedicated servants; by the household witness—“But if his shirt is torn from behind, then she lies and he tells the truth” (12:27); by Potiphar’s rebuke, “This is from you women’s guile” (12:28); by the woman’s later confession, “Now the truth has come to light! It was I who solicited him, and he is indeed telling the truth” (12:51); by the townswomen’s declaration that they knew no evil in him; and by Joseph’s own statement, “I did not betray him in his absence” (12:52).

According to Al-Mizan, the root of the erroneous view is, first, an indiscriminate acceptance of transmitted tales even when they conflict with reason and explicit Qur’anic texts. Those who do so reduce prophethood, sainthood, infallibility, and sincerity to socially imagined titles with no real spiritual basis, measuring prophets by the unstable souls of ordinary people. They can then conceive divine protection only as a coercive barrier that cancels other inclinations and compels good. But a compelled act has neither beauty nor merit and cannot warrant praise. The commentary associates this approach with acceptance of predestination (jabr), whereas the proponents of divine justice and monotheism do not accept such false attributions to God and His prophets.

The second source of error is a grammatical reading that treats “and he would have made for her” as an independent, completed assertion and takes the unstated result of “had he not beheld the proof of his Lord” to mean that he would have yielded. Al-Mizan judges this flawed. Both “she certainly made for him” and “he would have made for her” fall under the oath-like emphasis, and the latter clause is joined to the former; the conditional’s consequence is understood, as in saying, “By God, I would have hit him had he hit me.” There is no contextual reason to split the two clauses into independent statements.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī offer a different defence of Joseph: his hamm was merely a natural sexual inclination, not a deliberate resolve, and his reward lay in restraining it. Al-Mizan objects that natural appetite is not called hamm. Hamm linguistically denotes intention toward an act, accompanied by some revealing movement or preliminary, and such an intention would be blameworthy in a prophet even if involuntary natural urges themselves are not morally accountable. The commentary finally distinguishes the woman’s hamm as her deliberate approach to intimacy from Joseph’s, in the actual event, as no more than consideration without realization; it cannot be interpreted as an actual sinful resolve. His lavish divine praise rules out such a resolve. At the same time, the conditional wording preserves that, without the proof, he would have approached the act.

Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, proposes that the two instances of hamm refer to different acts: she intended fornication, while Joseph intended to strike or repel her. On this reading, the proof warned him that retaliation would bring destruction, murder, or a false accusation, and “evil and indecency” would mean those consequences. Al-Mizan replies that there is nothing intrinsically impossible in both parties simultaneously intending intimacy without its occurring; two people may both move toward one another at once. Differentiating the two uses of hamm departs from the apparent text without necessity, and making the proof a warning about retaliation, and evil and indecency murder and slander, conflicts with the passage’s context.

Rashīd Riḍā in Tafsīr al-Manār similarly interprets both instances of hamm as an intention to strike: the woman, angered by Joseph’s refusal, meant to punish him, while Joseph prepared to defend himself but fled when God showed him that resistance would lead to accusation. He also argues that a woman’s role in intimacy is passive, that Joseph did not initiate such an act, that the wording would otherwise put Joseph first, and that her settled determination does not fit the tentative sense of hamm. Al-Mizan treats this as substantially the same unsupported non-carnal interpretation. The narrative supplies no evidence that she intended to strike him; intimate conduct can involve active initiative by a woman; and her firm desire for Joseph did not ensure that he would reciprocate or that the act would occur. Her rebuff by Joseph explains why her intent could remain an unfulfilled hamm.

Another view, attributed by al-Ṭabrisī to Abū Muslim, rearranges the verse to mean that Joseph would have made for her had he not seen the proof, but did not do so because he saw it. Al-Mizan replies that the alleged reversals of Qur’anic order concern separate sentences or enumerated matters, not a construction in which changing the syntactical order changes whether hamm is qualified by law lā. Classical Arabic grammar does not permit the consequent of this conditional to precede its condition; only an implied consequent is possible where the context indicates it.

Al-Ghazālī also reports a dream interpretation: Joseph saw the woman in a dream, inferred that she was meant for him, and was consequently attracted to her. Al-Mizan rejects this as textual speculation. If the dream itself is meant by his hamm, it lacks evidence; if he treated a prophetic dream as revelation and then discovered that it was mistaken, the interpretation implies error in receiving revelation, which is no less unacceptable than imputing sin to a prophet. It also contradicts Joseph’s own prior recognition that the proposed intimacy was wrongdoing from which he sought God’s refuge.

Other explanations make the proof a physical warning, knowledge of the prohibition and punishment of fornication, chastity (ʿiffa), spiritual purity, or infallibility. Al-Mizan maintains instead that the verse itself indicates a divinely shown, witnessed certainty through which God wards inclination and adultery away from His exclusively devoted servant.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains that istibāq means that Joseph and Potiphar’s wife each tried to outrun the other, but for opposite purposes: Joseph sought to open the door and escape the house, while she sought to stop him from leaving and obtain what she wanted. Joseph reached the door first, but she pulled his shirt from behind as he fled, ripping it lengthwise. Qadd denotes such a lengthwise tear, unlike qaṭṭ, a tear across the width; dubur means the back, in contrast to the front. The direction of the tear thus accords with Joseph’s flight from her.

They then found her husband at the door: alfayā means to find, and sayyid, literally “master,” here means her spouse. His arrival transformed the private encounter into a confrontation. The wife immediately accused Joseph indirectly, demanding punishment for whoever intended evil toward “your wife,” whether imprisonment or a painful punishment. Without naming Joseph, herself, or the alleged harm—adultery—she framed a general rule, maintaining decorum toward her husband while seeking to incite him against Joseph. Her failure to specify either the charge or punishment reflects her attachment to Joseph and the consolation of ambiguity; her wording was a ruse to divert her husband’s attention from her own guilt and shift blame onto him.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph had initially remained silent out of respect for Potiphar and to shield his wife from blame, but her accusation required him to state the truth: “It was she who solicited me.” His unembellished statement, without emphatic particles or an oath, shows his restraint and composure. Having done no wrong and already sought refuge in his Lord—“God forbid!.”—he was neither ashamed, frightened, nor ingratiating in denying her charge.

The witness’s “testified” means “said”; the statement itself contains what is called testimony. It supplies a decisive physical indication that one of the two parties is truthful: a shirt torn at the front would imply a face-to-face struggle and support the wife’s accusation, whereas a shirt torn from behind shows that Joseph was fleeing and she was pursuing and pulling him back. Thus the latter condition establishes her falsehood and Joseph’s truthfulness.

Commentators differ over the witness’s identity. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and ʿIkrima are reported to have regarded him as a wise adviser of Potiphar; others call him a male relative of the wife who was with her husband at the door. Mujāhid is cited as saying that he was neither human nor jinn but a distinct creation of God, though this conflicts with the explicit description, “from her own household.” Traditions from the Household of the Prophet, along with some Sunnī sources, report that he was an infant from her family still in the cradle.

The evidence offered is rational inference leading conclusively to one party’s guilt, whereas shahāda ordinarily rests on sensory perception or its equivalent, not reflection. In such usages as “their hearing will bear witness against them and their sight and their skins (41:20)” and “When the hypocrites come to you they say, ‘We bear witness that you are indeed the messenger of Allah.’ (63:1),” testimony expresses an established truth without emphasizing the reasoning behind it; a deliberate, reflective utterance is otherwise called qawl. It is also possible that “A witness … testified” means that the speaker uttered this spontaneously and without forethought, making it shahāda rather than qawl. This reading accords with the narration of the cradled infant and may indicate a miracle by which God supported Joseph’s claim.

verses.28: Al-Mizan explains that, on seeing Joseph’s shirt torn from behind, Potiphar recognized that his wife’s accusation was a scheme and took Joseph’s side. He ascribed it collectively to women because he regarded it as arising from a woman’s nature: women can allure men, who are naturally drawn to them, ensnaring their hearts and turning them toward desire without their noticing. Such guile is meant to harm men.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan holds that this is Potiphar’s speech after he judged in Joseph’s favour: he tells Joseph to dismiss the incident, treat it as though it had not occurred, and not disclose it, while ordering his wife to seek forgiveness for her sin. Joseph’s conduct accords with this, for he did not accuse her when they were discovered until she charged him with intending harm; nevertheless, her prolonged and overpowering infatuation could not have remained secret, as the later gossip of the city women shows.

The command confirms the woman’s guilt. The masculine plural min al-khātiʾīn includes both men and women, hence it is used rather than the feminine khātiʾāt. The whole statement belongs to Potiphar, not the witness, since Potiphar rendered the judgement. Thus the interpretation that she is being told to ask her husband not to punish her, based on assigning the words to the witness, is mistaken.

The command may be understood as seeking God’s forgiveness and repenting, since Egyptians acknowledged God as Creator despite worshipping other deities. Yet the verse does not specify from whom she must seek forgiveness; within her religion, it would be the deity she worshipped. Finally, the verse does not indicate that Potiphar lacked jealousy, but rather that he loved his wife deeply.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse begins the six-verse account of the women of Egypt and Joseph in the house of Potiphar. News of the incident with Potiphar’s wife gradually spread through the city, and its elite women discussed her in their gatherings. They derided her as one overcome by love for a young servant and persistently trying to seduce him, judging her to be in manifest error. Their talk was a ruse against her, arising from envy, pride, and resentment: they had neither seen Joseph nor experienced what she had, but merely speculated. The commentary observes that delicate emotions, beauty, and attraction can, especially among young women, foster self-conceit and envy.

When the gossip reached Potiphar’s wife, her overriding concern was that Joseph should yield to her and love her in return, rather than her rank or public standing. Recognizing the women’s scheme, she invited these noblewomen, who were socially connected with Potiphar’s household, to a gathering. They attended in their finest dress, hoping to see the beauty that had exposed her. Her purpose was to show them Joseph so that they would understand her infatuation and cease focusing on her indiscretion. She felt secure in her authority as his mistress and owner, believed that he had no interest in other women, and knew his resistance to temptation.

After seating them and providing fruit and knives, she summoned Joseph, who had been kept from their sight. On seeing him, the women were so astonished that they cut their hands instead of the fruit. Intense desire, fear, or surprise can disorient a person, causing unintentional and even harmful actions. Potiphar’s wife’s attachment had grown gradually, whereas the women were suddenly overwhelmed by Joseph’s beauty; their reason and discernment failed, and they openly exclaimed, ‘Good heavens! This is not a human being! This is but a noble angel!’

Their conduct was especially striking because it occurred in Potiphar’s house, where decorum was expected. They were noble, beautiful, married women known for modesty and chastity; they had themselves recently condemned Potiphar’s wife, although she had lived with Joseph for years. Yet Joseph’s beauty erased their former judgment, and the gathering became an open display of their emotions before Joseph himself. Their exclamation amounted to an unwitting confession: their earlier blame would have been valid had Joseph been an ordinary human being, for a person may be blamed for desiring another human when an equally attractive alternative is available. But, in the commentary’s presentation, unmatched, supernatural beauty that weakens resolve and choice excuses one who succumbs to its attraction.

The women then spoke freely of Joseph’s attractiveness. Potiphar’s wife admitted what she had previously concealed: ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me. Certainly I did solicit him, but he was continent’ (12:32). To preserve her standing among them and seek Joseph’s compliance, she threatened him with imprisonment and abasement. Joseph, however, was unaffected by the women’s allure, glances, and speech, and by her threat. His attention was fixed upon the Beauty before which all other beauty vanishes and the Majesty before which all power and dignity are humbled. Rather than respond to them, he prayed: ‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them and become one of the senseless’ (12:33).

Al-Mizan holds that this trial was more severe than the earlier private attempt by Potiphar’s wife. Joseph now faced the open professions, collective desire, and intrigues of the townswomen, who sought to tempt and seduce him. He therefore fervently asked God to avert their schemes; whereas he had previously only sought God’s protection, God answered this prayer by turning their schemes away from him.

The commentary explains that niswa means a group of women, while fī al-madīna indicates that they were sufficiently numerous or influential for the scandal to become widespread. Imraʾat al-ʿazīz is the wife of the master in whose house Joseph lived and who sought to seduce him. The title ʿazīz was used for the master who bought Joseph from the caravan, for Egyptian dignitaries, and later for Joseph when he was placed over the land’s granaries. Turāwid conveys the continuity and intensification of seduction, murāwada. Although fatā ordinarily means a young man, here it means a servant, hence ‘her slave boy.’

Concerning shaghafa-hā ḥubban, al-Rāghib reports in his Mufradāt that, according to al-Ḥasan, passion had reached the innermost part of her heart, while Abū ʿAlī understood it as its centre; the two meanings are similar. Other interpretations identify it with the heart’s enveloping layer. Thus, the women’s influential speech reproached a noblewoman for trying to seduce, and becoming infatuated with, a foreign servant despite his refusals. As the chief’s wife, she should have guarded her household’s honour, her husband’s dignity, and her own reputation; her persistent solicitation was deemed reprehensible and a departure from good sense. This is why, after saying that she solicited her slave boy, they concluded, ‘Indeed we see her to be in manifest error.’
verses.31:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī’s definition of makr as a covert stratagem for attaining one’s aim, explains that the women’s gossip was called machinations because it was intended to shame the wife of Potiphar publicly and diminish her standing, out of jealousy and malice. She summoned them to show them Joseph’s beauty and make them experience the trial that had overcome her, so that they would cease blaming her and understand her infatuation. Another view holds that the women used their remarks as a pretext to secure an invitation, having heard of Joseph’s extraordinary beauty, in order to see him and perhaps seduce him themselves; but Al-Mizan judges the first explanation more consonant with the verses’ context.

Her sending for them simply means inviting them to gather before her. In arranging a repast (aʿtaddat la-hunnā muttakaʾan), she prepared what was needed for reclining, such as cushions or seats customary in elite homes; some interpret muttakaʾ as citrus fruit. Giving each woman a knife indicates fruit or similar food set before them to cut and eat. Her command, ‘Come out before them,’ ordered Joseph to appear. Its wording suggests that he had been concealed within the house, perhaps in an adjoining room; if he had been outside, she would have said, ‘Enter upon them’ (idkhil ʿalay-hinna).

Al-Mizan presents the gathering as her deliberate counter-strategy: she prepared their places and knives, kept Joseph from view, and suddenly revealed him so that his beauty would overwhelm them and vindicate her in their eyes. All of them, not merely one or two, cut their hands. This illustrates that when an overwhelming beauty or grandeur confronts something lesser, it can dominate the senses, displace other concerns, and cause unintentional acts. Thus they cut their hands rather than the fruit. The emphatic form qaṭṭaʿa further conveys the repeated or excessive character of the cutting.

Their ‘Good heavens!’ (hāsha li llāh) glorifies God in connection with Joseph. In eloquent speech, one magnifies God before exonerating or exalting someone; thus, before declaring that Joseph was not human, they glorified God and then praised him. By calling him ‘a noble angel,’ they denied that he was an ordinary mortal and likened him to the blessed angels whom many, including pagans, regarded as sources of goodness, happiness, life, knowledge, beauty, radiance, and joy, and as possessing both physical and moral beauty. Although his outward appearance first struck them, their description of him as a noble angel perhaps alluded to the beauty of both his character and his form.

Finally, because their exclamation precedes the wife of Potiphar’s statement, ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me,’ it was not an intentional acknowledgment that her love was excusable. Rather, it was a spontaneous disclosure of their own admiration and infatuation. They exposed themselves both by cutting their hands and by praising Joseph, after which they could only acknowledge the truth of her statement and excuse her conduct.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse answers what Potiphar’s wife said after the women’s words and actions exposed their own attraction to Joseph. Pointing to him as the one for whom they had blamed her, she presented the very object of their accusation before them: the man for whose sake they alleged that she had abandoned household honour, her husband’s dignity, and her chastity.

She then disclosed what she had concealed: she had solicited Joseph, but he had remained continent and sought God’s protection. Seeing the women’s hearts incline towards him, she both shared her frustration and signalled to Joseph that she had not abandoned her purpose. Her declaration that, if he did not obey her, he would be imprisoned and abased (wa la-in lam yafʿal mā āmuru-hu la-yusjan-anna wa la-yakūnan min al-ṣāghirīn) is reinforced by oaths and emphatic particles, showing her unwavering resolve and her claim to possess the means to compel him. It is at once a boastful warning to the women and a direct threat to Joseph: disobedience would bring imprisonment after comfort and humiliation after honour.

The commentary distinguishes this from her earlier statement to her husband, “‘What is to be the requital of him who has evil intentions for your wife except imprisonment or a painful punishment?’ (12:25) There she left imprisonment and painful punishment as alternatives; here she joins imprisonment to abasement. Moreover, she now threatens him in her own name rather than appealing to her husband, displaying her conviction that she can sway her husband’s heart and direct his affairs according to her will.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains aṣbu as an inclination driven by desire: al-Rāghib relates it to ṣabā and cognate forms denoting being impelled by desire, while al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, calls ṣibwa “the subtleties of desire.” As Potiphar’s wife and the women disclosed their intentions and tempted Joseph, he gave them no reply but turned wholly to his Lord: “My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me.”

This opening is not a request to be imprisoned, nor a request that God protect him by putting him in prison. It candidly states his condition: owing to his divine upbringing, he judges the hardship of prison preferable to sin, which would estrange him from God. It resembles his earlier reply to Potiphar’s wife—“God forbid! Indeed He is my Lord; He has given me a good abode. Indeed the wrongdoers are not felicitous” (12:23)—in its rejection of sin and reliance on God, though the earlier statement addressed her and this one addresses God. Neither opening statement is itself a supplication. Rather, it prepares for the conditional plea, “If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them,” expressed as a statement of his need.

Joseph means that, if forced to choose between prison and their invitation, he would choose prison. He asks God to avert their schemes, for without the divinely granted knowledge that protects him, he might be drawn by desire and become one of the senseless. His preference does not mean that their invitation is desirable in itself; it can appeal only through human nature and the low self (al-nafs al-ammāra), which incites evil. Thus “So his Lord answered him …” (12:34) answers the plea to turn away their schemes, as the verse itself says that God turned their stratagems from him; it does not answer an alleged prayer for imprisonment. His later confinement—“Then it appeared to them, after they had seen all the signs, that they should confine him for some time” (12:35)—would not have been described in this way had it been the object of his supplication and God’s decree in response.

The commentary holds that the women, like Potiphar’s wife, apparently tried to seduce Joseph. The verse does not settle whether each invited him to herself, to Potiphar’s wife, or both; but his fear that he might incline “towards them” indicates invitations from them. His later reference to “women who cut their hands,” and the wife’s confession—“Now the truth has come to light! It was I who solicited him, and he is indeed telling the truth” … “that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not further the schemes of the treacherous” (12:50-52)—suggest that the women were involved in the plot to invite him to her. The singular in “I did not betray him in his absence” points particularly to Potiphar’s wife. Moreover, it is highly improbable that women so overwhelmed by Joseph that they cut their hands would simply leave him alone; their infatuation would normally lead them to pursue their desire by every available means. Joseph’s private turn from them to God therefore manifests the extremity of the trial and calamity they imposed upon him.

The strength by which Joseph was protected was not an innate, self-sufficient possession, but a divine aid bestowed upon him repeatedly and gradually. This is indicated by his present-tense condition, “If You do not turn away their schemes from me,” rather than a formulation referring to protection already completed. Accordingly, God’s turning their stratagems away is a new divine act answering his prayer.

Finally, that Joseph says he would become one of the senseless (jāhilīn), rather than wrongdoers (ẓālimīn) or treacherous (khāʾinīn), shows that this divine strength belongs to knowledge and thought. In speaking to the women, he described the outward character of the act at their level of understanding: it is wrongdoing, whose perpetrators are not felicitous, and treachery, whose schemes God does not further. In addressing his Lord, however, he identifies its true reality: inclination towards them arises from ignorance.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains that God answered Joseph’s plea that the women’s schemes be turned away from him, expressed in, “If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them …” God’s names, the All-hearing and the All-knowing, show that He hears His servants’ speech and knows their condition.

Law, noble ethics, and monotheism are inseparable in the proper order: law can flourish only through faith protected by noble character, and noble character is completed only by monotheistic belief. Monotheism is the root of the tree of human happiness, while piety, chastity, knowledge, courage, justice, and mercy are among its branches; true belief ascends to God, and righteous conduct raises it. Human beings need cooperative society because no one can independently perform all the tasks of life. They therefore require laws that preserve rights, regulate exchange and work, and prevent the strong from oppressing the weak. Laws also need penalties, encouragement toward good, and a governing power able to know crimes and enforce justice.

Yet laws cannot enforce themselves. If their enforcer is ignorant, weak, negligent, or overcome by criminals, corruption and violations of rights spread; people naturally tend to seek their own benefit even at others’ expense. Excessive concentration of power can likewise leave people unable to correct injustice, producing an unchallengeable authority. History and present conditions alike display tyrannical domination. Thus, even just laws and severe punishments cannot secure society without morals that oppose oppression and corruption and uphold truth, human dignity, justice, life, and compassion.

The apparent order and justice of advanced nations should not deceive one. Their people may act collectively for the welfare of their own nation, but this commonly entails exploiting weaker nations through subjugation, colonization, and the violation of their rights. What former tyrants did to individuals is now done by nations to other societies, while such terms as freedom, honour, justice, and virtue may be used for their opposites.

Even morality cannot truly bring happiness or lead a person to righteous action unless founded on monotheism: belief in the one eternal God, from whom nothing is hidden, whose power surpasses creation, who orders it by His will, and to whom all return for recompense—eternal bliss for the virtuous and perpetual torment for wrongdoers. Morality rooted in this belief makes seeking God’s approval one’s concern, and taqwā becomes an inward restraint from evil. Without it, people seek transient worldly pleasure. At most, they may obey public norms to preserve society, gain its benefits, or win praise and historical renown. But praise generally concerns conspicuous major deeds, while hidden acts are unprotected by public regard; great renown also demands sacrifices that a person who believes death ends all benefit has no rational motive to make. Such considerations cannot replace monotheism or prevent concealed wrongdoing, especially where circumstances can make upright conduct appear blameworthy. Joseph’s refusal to betray Potiphar was falsely portrayed by Potiphar’s wife as aggression against her; nothing prevented him from sin except knowledge of his Lord’s station.

Religious piety, or worship, follows one of three paths: fear (khawf), hope (rajāʾ), and love (ḥubb). The believer must recognize worldly life as fleeting play, adornment, rivalry, and covetousness, rather than make it the final aim. He fears the punishment due to wrongdoing, hopes for God’s forgiveness and reward for righteousness, and gives God’s pleasure precedence over self-satisfaction. Most worship from fear: reflecting on the punishment promised to sinners strengthens their fear and moves them to obedience. Others worship chiefly from hope: reflecting on promised blessing, honour, forgiveness, and Paradise increases their piety and good works.

Those who truly know God worship neither merely to escape punishment nor to obtain reward, but because He is worthy of worship. Knowing Him by His fitting names and attributes, they recognize Him as their Lord and the governor of all reality, while they themselves are servants whose duty is to prefer His will to their own. They seek His countenance in action and abstention alike. Fear of His punishment and hope for His mercy may remain, but do not constitute the motive of their worship. As the saying puts it: “I did not worship You out of fear of Your Hell, or for the desire of Your Paradise. Rather, I found You worthy of worship, so I worshipped You.”

When people subordinate their desires to God’s pleasure and seek God Himself as their end, love of Him arises from knowing Him through His most beautiful names and attributes of perfection. Human nature is drawn to beauty, and God is Absolute Beauty. Created things are signs of His beauty and majesty: through their created beauty they proclaim His praise, and through their limitation and need they indicate His absolute sufficiency, sanctity, power, and grandeur. One who regards things as signs rather than independently desired objects is drawn to divine greatness, forgets self and personal whims, and acquires a heart devoted entirely to God. This is the meaning of the more ardent love of God possessed by the faithful.

From this standpoint, worship from fear or hope is not wholly free of associating partners with God, because the worshipper seeks protection, favour, honour, or reward rather than God Himself; if these could be obtained without worship, such a person would not seek to know Him. A narration from al-Ṣādiq says, “Is religion (dīn) anything other than love (ḥubb)?” Another tradition from him states: “Indeed, I worship Him out of love for Him, and this is a hidden station that can only be reached by the purified.” Those who truly love God are purified of selfish desire and material inclination, and complete sincerity in worship is attained through love.

Worship motivated by fear leads to renunciation (zuhd): abstaining from worldly matters in order to secure salvation, and avoiding prohibited acts and what resembles them, namely neglect of obligations. Worship motivated by hope leads to active righteous deeds for the blessings of the hereafter, including fulfilment of obligations and avoidance of prohibitions. Both yield devotion to religion rather than devotion to the Lord of religion.

Love of God, however, cleanses the heart of attachment to everything besides Him: worldly adornment, family, wealth, status, and even one’s own aspirations. It binds the heart to God and to all that is related to Him—His religion, prophet, saint, and whatever traces back to Him—because love of someone entails love of what belongs to him. The lover therefore prefers what God loves, hates what He disapproves, is pleased by what pleases Him and angered by what angers Him. This love is the light and spirit by which one acts, so that goodness and beauty proceed from him and evil is avoided.

Such a person sees every created thing and event, great or small, as a pure sign of absolute beauty, rather than as something defective or repulsive in itself. He is consequently encompassed by divine blessing: joy without sorrow, pleasure without pain, and security without fear, since sorrow and fear arise from seeing evil or expecting harm. This state exceeds ordinary understanding. These people are God’s friends, the nearest to Him, with no obstruction from sense, illusion, personal whim, or satanic insinuation. They see every perception as a sign unveiling divine truth and possess the knowledge of certitude (ʿilm al-yaqīn), through which hidden realities are unveiled. They truly rely on God, trust Him, are content with His decree, and submit to His will. Seeing His goodness and beauty in all things, they acquire noble qualities in accordance with this high monotheism and devote both their ethics and deeds wholly to God.

The servant’s devotion (ikhlāṣ) is itself God’s grace, for the servant possesses no spiritual blessing independently of Him. God created some servants with upright natures, balanced temperaments, sound intellects, pure souls, and wholesome hearts. Because of this original purity, they attain a level of sincerity that others may seek through striving, but in a more elevated form because they are free from obstructions and distractions. It appears that these are the Qurʾanic mukhlaṣūn, God’s “exclusive servants”: the prophets and the imāms, whom God chose, gathered for Himself, and purified for His presence.

God gives them a knowledge that shields them from every minor and major sin. This is infallibility (ʿiṣma), distinct from moral rectitude (ʿadāla): both prevent sinful acts, but infallibility also prevents contemplation of sin. The exclusive servants possess a knowledge from their Lord unlike that of others; divine love makes them desire only what God desires, and Satan himself excepts God’s exclusive servants from those he can pervert. Joseph’s words—“My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline toward them and become one of the senseless” (12:33)—also indicate this distinctive knowledge. Unlike ordinary knowledge, which may influence conduct without doing so invariably, it decisively and continuously directs one away from what is improper and toward what is proper. People may possess ordinary knowledge and nevertheless knowingly reject truth, follow desire, or differ out of envy.

Although revelation and rational proof provide knowledge of God’s names and attributes, God’s transcendence exceeds every description except those supplied by His exclusive servants. Thus, knowledge of the same subject is not always equal in kind or effect.

The knowledge constituting ʿiṣma does not change human nature, remove voluntary action, or impose compulsion. A person who knows a drink to be deadly poison avoids it freely; knowledge does not itself force the will, and compulsion occurs only where one possible alternative is made impossible. The fact that the chosen and guided retain the capacity to ascribe partners to God, though divine guidance keeps them from doing so, confirms this. The infallible refrains from sin through his own choice and will, just as ordinary people may receive divine favour assisting them to abstain from sin.

Nor is this contradicted by the Qurʾanic and traditional teaching that prophets and imāms are guided by the Holy Spirit (rūh al-qudus). This is comparable to attributing a believer’s guidance to the spirit of faith or a person’s misguidance to the devil: it does not remove the act from the agent’s own choice and will.

Al-Mizan rejects the view of theologians who say that God diverts a person from sin by interrupting natural causes—such as giving a contrary will, sending an angel to overpower a person’s will, or permitting Satan to turn a person from good to evil.
