Their underlying outlook, tending toward determinism, treats things as needing God only at their inception and then as independent within causal sequence, though subject to His occasional intervention. Direct human experience refutes this: in good and evil action, one does not find an external force competing with or overpowering the self; one acts according to one’s feelings and the choice arising from them. Angels and devils, insofar as they affect the soul, are longitudinal causes rather than transversal ones. Qurʾanic monotheism and its related doctrines likewise refute that view at its root.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains badāʾ as a new opinion arising after an event. “Them” denotes Potiphar, his wife, and their informed associates; the “signs” were proofs of Joseph’s innocence and continence, including the boy’s testimony, the shirt torn from behind, and their arrival at the door, and perhaps also the women’s reaction, Joseph’s refusal, and the wife’s admission that she had sought to seduce him.

The oath-form in la-yasjununna-hu shows that, despite this evidence, they jointly resolved to imprison him temporarily, until the city’s rumors of seduction had faded. The decision served Potiphar’s household by shielding it from disgrace and perhaps also by preventing the disturbance Joseph’s beauty might cause among the people.

The later inquiry into the women who cut their hands suggests that Potiphar’s wife subsequently misled her husband about the evidence, perhaps causing him to doubt Joseph’s innocence. Al-Mizan therefore considers it likely that she facilitated or ordered the imprisonment both to divert blame from herself and to punish Joseph in the hope that confinement would make him yield to her commands.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that fatayān means slaves, and the context, supported by narrations, indicates that the two men entering prison with Joseph were servants of the king. One related a dream of pressing grapes for wine—khamr being used in view of the grapes’ eventual product—and the other a dream of carrying bread on his head while birds pecked at it.

They asked Joseph for the interpretation of their respective dreams because the signs of virtue they perceived in him led them to regard him as a trustworthy and insightful man. The commentary also notes the Qurʾan’s stylistic elegance in not explicitly repeating “they said” before their joint request.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan states that Joseph used his fellow prisoners’ esteem for his moral character and their request for dream interpretation as an occasion to call them to monotheism. He attributed his knowledge to his Lord’s teaching, rejected the creed of those without faith in Allah and the Hereafter, and then proceeded to interpret the dreams.

The preferred reading takes “its interpretation” to refer to the food that would be brought to them: before their meal arrived, Joseph would tell them its nature and outcome. This would be a sign of his prophethood and of the truth of his monotheistic summons, and narrations from the Household of the Prophet support it. If the pronoun instead refers to the dreams, Joseph merely promises a prompt interpretation, but Al-Mizan considers this less likely in the context.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph’s ability to interpret dreams was not acquired knowledge but teaching from God, bestowed in connection with his rejection of idolatry and adherence to the monotheistic creed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This is also Joseph’s first open declaration in Egypt of his descent from that family.

Though idolaters may affirm God and a recompense through reincarnation, the commentary holds that associating partners with God, whether in influence or worship, is not true belief in Him; reincarnation likewise conflicts with resurrection and return to God for final judgment. Thus Joseph’s words deny that such people truly believe in God or the Hereafter.

“It is not for us to ascribe any partner to Allah” means that God has protected the prophetic Household from idolatry. This is not compulsion (ijbār), but divine guidance (tasdīd) and support (taʾyīd), granted with prophethood and messengership; they seek God’s protection and hold to monotheism. The usual explanation is that this is a favor to them through support with truth and a favor to people because they can follow the prophets to salvation. Most people are ungrateful by neglecting the messengers or by worshipping angels, jinn, or humans besides God.

Al-Mizan adds that monotheism and the negation of partners are not derived from prophetic teaching alone: reason and innate human nature know them. People and prophets therefore stand under the same divine law of monotheism, and people’s deviation results from failing to heed their natural disposition, not merely from failing to follow prophets.

Just as divine care requires equipping humanity with reason and revelation, it requires raising individuals of pure soul and sound heart who preserve, defend, and teach monotheism. Otherwise, since what may befall one person may befall all, universal polytheism would corrupt humanity and frustrate creation’s purpose. These individuals—surely the prophets and Imāms—relate to the public through teaching and learning, continually recalling people to a truth obscured by material and sensual preoccupations. Their creation and mission are therefore a grace to them, through God’s teaching of His oneness, and to humankind, through their reminder, instruction, and correction. The verse does not refer to dream interpretation as the divine grace; that reading is remote from its context.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains khayr here as what is preferable to choose in the relevant respect; between deities, it concerns the choice of what should be worshipped. Joseph’s question is therefore an argument requiring worship of the true Lord alone, not merely an assertion that God exists or is the highest deity.

He calls the objects of polytheistic worship arbāb mutafarriqūn, “different masters,” because idolaters divided supposed divine attributes and manifestations among distinct beings and idols: angels assigned particular domains, jinn regarded as sources of evils, and holy men, rulers, and kings. Against these separate beings, Joseph invokes Allah as “the One, the All-paramount.”

God’s absolute and unbounded existence excludes limitation, decay, dependence, and division. His perfections—such as life, knowledge, and power—are neither additions to nor parts of His essence, but are intrinsically identical with it. He is one not as a numerical unit to which another could be added, but such that no independent essence or attribute can be posited beside Him. Nothing dominates Him, and no real distinction can be made between His essence and His attributes or among the attributes themselves.

Accordingly, worship of multiple deities, or of one divine attribute apart from God’s essence, is impossible; worship of the essence entails worship of the attributes. The idolaters’ claim that God is too transcendent to approach directly and that noble creatures should be worshipped as intercessors is taken up and refuted in the following statement, “You do not worship besides Him but names …”
verses.40:
Al-Mizan notes that Joseph’s address expands from his two prison companions to all idolaters, since its rule is universal. What they worship besides God are only names coined by them and their forefathers, with no real entities established behind them. Allah has sent down no sulṭān—no rationally compelling proof—either for such beings’ alleged divinity or, possibly, for worshipping them as independent influences or intercessors.

“Sovereignty belongs only to Allah” establishes that all true decree belongs to the One who governs worldly affairs and guides His servants. It both explains why no authority exists for those fabricated objects of worship and answers the implicit question of what God has decreed: He has commanded worship of none but Himself. Hence it is invalid to worship such alleged intermediaries or seek their intercession in hope of benefit or fear of harm.

“That is the upright religion” refers to God’s transcendent oneness and the rejection of partners. Al-dīn al-qayyim is firm, self-standing, and able to order society and lead it to felicity, because sound social norms must rest on realities rather than myths. Most people do not know this because absorption in the passing sensory world deprives them of a pure heart and clear understanding and turns them away from the Hereafter.

The commentary treats Joseph’s words from “O my prison mates!” through the command to worship God alone as one argument for monotheistic worship. God’s intrinsic, necessary divinity entails that He is singular and all-dominant, with no second or independent co-influencer. Nor is there divine proof for a divinity of intercession by others; reason and the prophets’ teaching alike require worship of Him alone.

Al-Mizan rejects al-Bayḍāwī’s, following al-Zamakhsharī, division of the two verses into a merely rhetorical proof followed by a logical proof. This overlooks “the One, the All-paramount” and assigns to the second verse alone a conclusion that follows from both together. It also rejects an alternative reading that makes the first verse a proof from the harmony of cosmic causes against discordant gods and the second a general denial of every other deity. That reading improperly limits the unqualified meaning of “the All-paramount,” who dominates all things in their essences, attributes, and effects, and it generalizes the second verse beyond its concern with divinity by God’s permission—namely, alleged intercession—into intrinsic divinity.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph interpreted the dream of pressing wine as the prisoner’s return to serving wine to his master, and the dream of birds eating bread from the other prisoner’s head as his crucifixion and the birds’ eating from his head.

“The matter about which you inquire has been decided” suggests that one or both men may have disowned the dream related to Joseph, perhaps the man who heard the sentence of crucifixion. A narration from the Imāms of the Household of the Prophet reports that this man said he had lied about his dream; Joseph’s reply means that the interpretation sought was nevertheless definite and inevitable.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan takes the pronouns in “he said,” “he knew,” and “he remained” to refer to Joseph. He asked the prisoner whom he knew would be delivered to mention him to his master, so that the master might show mercy and release him. In this context ẓanna means belief in a general sense, without specifying its degree of certainty; it does not show that Joseph’s interpretation rested on personal reasoning, since he had declared the matter decided and God had taught him dream interpretation. A possible alternative is that the saved prisoner, rather than Joseph, was the one who believed himself saved on the basis of Joseph’s interpretation.

The pronouns in “Satan caused him to forget mentioning it to his master” refer to the delivered prisoner: Satan made him forget to mention Joseph, leaving Joseph in prison for several years, biʿḍ denoting fewer than ten. The interpretation that Satan made Joseph forget God because he sought help from another person is rejected. God declares Joseph one of His exclusive, devoted servants, over whom Satan has no sway; moreover, devotion to God does not require abandoning ordinary means, but only refusing to rely on them instead of God. Nothing in Joseph’s request implies such reliance, and “Said the one of the two who had been delivered, remembering after a long time” (12:45) strongly confirms that the cupbearer, not Joseph, was the one who forgot.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that the king recounts a dream to his council, as shown by his request for an opinion on his dream and by arā, “I saw,” which may even suggest a recurring vision. simān is the plural of samīna, “fat,” and ʿijāf the exceptional plural of ʿajfāʾ, “lean” or “emaciated.” aftūnī asks for a judgment or response, while taʿburūn denotes interpreting a dream by passing from its visible form to the reality it represents.

The commentary reports al-Zamakhsharī’s grammatical explanation that simān qualifies baqarāt, identifying seven cows of the particular kind “fat,” rather than characterizing the number seven itself. Likewise, ʿijāf cannot serve as the specification of a number because it does not identify a species, unlike adjectival terms that function as nouns, such as “horsemen.”

Although the construction strongly inclines one to understand “others dry” as seven dry ears corresponding to the seven green ears, the verse does not conclusively establish this. Grammatically attaching “others dry” to “seven green ears” would be contradictory: “others” distinguishes them from the seven, rather than dividing one set of seven into green and dry ears. Thus the king asks his courtiers to interpret his vision of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, seven green ears, and other dry ones.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that aḥlām is the plural of ḥulum/ḥulm, what is seen in sleep. Its connection with ḥilm, soundness and steadiness of thought, also underlies its uses for mental maturity and forbearance. Citing al-Rāghib, the commentary notes that ḍighth is a bundle of herbs, grass, or twigs; aḍghāth aḥlām therefore portrays a tangled bundle of visions whose realities are obscure.

Calling the king’s vision “confused nightmares” emphasizes scattered and intermingled dream-images, each potentially requiring its own interpretation. The indefinite expression aḍghāth aḥlām reinforces this sense of a mixed collection, though the preceding verse does not explicitly establish that the king saw only one dream.

The definite al-aḥlām may mean that the courtiers could not interpret these particular confused dreams; if taken generally, it means they lacked knowledge of dream interpretation altogether. The latter can coexist with their calling the vision confused, whereas claiming ignorance only of genuine dreams would disconnect the two parts of their answer. They thus dismiss what he saw as a mishmash of visions which they cannot interpret, while implying that they interpret favorable visions.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that umma, though usually denoting a community united by a purpose, here means a period of years. The cupbearer who had been saved from prison then remembered Joseph and the request Joseph had made of him. His Satan-influenced forgetfulness had caused Joseph to remain imprisoned for further years.

He therefore tells those present that he can obtain the dream’s interpretation and asks to be sent to Joseph. The plural forms in “I will inform you” and “let me go” address not only the king but the influential officials attending him.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan notes that the Qurʾan abbreviates the intervening narrative: the cupbearer was sent to Joseph in prison, addressed him as “truthful,” recounted the king’s vision, and indicated that people awaited its meaning. Joseph is called ṣiddīq because of his constant and exacting truthfulness in his interpretations, conduct, and speech during imprisonment; God affirms this quality without qualification.

Though the request does not expressly call the account a dream, aftinā seeks an interpretive judgment, and the earlier encounter between the cupbearer and Joseph makes its subject clear. The cupbearer asks for an interpretation so that he may return with it and enable the people to understand the vision and escape their confusion.

His wording shows that he seeks the answer on behalf of the king and council, rather than for private knowledge; accordingly, Joseph’s reply addresses a plurality. Saying that he will return “to the people,” rather than merely to the king or courtiers, further suggests that news of the king’s dream had spread and that the public awaited an explanation. It may also indicate the council’s concern for the people, since a king’s dreams naturally concern the affairs of his realm and subjects.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains sabʿa sinīna daʾban as seven years of continuous, successive cultivation: daʾb denotes a constant course, habit, or pattern. Some interpret it as strenuous labor, or as an adverb requiring persistent diligence. The statement “You will sow” may also be phrased declaratively while functioning as a command, to stress the necessity of compliance.

They are then instructed to keep harvested grain in its ears, apart from the small amount consumed. Stored in the ear, grain is less liable to pests and decay than when threshed and cleaned. Thus Joseph directs them to sow continually for seven years and preserve the crop in this form so that it will not perish.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains sabʿun shidād as seven severe years of drought and famine. Shidād may simply mean difficult, or may evoke years that “attack” the people; the latter accords with their being said to consume the provisions stored for them, like predatory beasts consuming what is offered to them. tuḥṣinūn means to preserve and save. After the fruitful years, the seven hard years will consume the prepared stores, except for the small portion that is kept safe.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains that yughāth al-nās can mean that people are granted relief from distress, or that they receive rain; it may also be connected with ghayth, vegetation produced by rain. Rain is more fitting with “in which they will press,” unless yaʿṣirūn is read passively as meaning that they will be rained upon. The objection that Egypt depends on the Nile rather than rain is rejected, since the Nile’s flooding depends on rainwater flowing into it from Sudan.

yaʿṣirūn derives from ʿaṣr, pressing juice or oil from such things as grapes, dates, olives, or sesame; it may also mean milking livestock. The verse therefore foretells renewed produce, rainfall or relief, and an abundance enabling people to press juices and oils or milk their animals.

The commentary distinguishes its position from al-Bayḍāwī’s possibilities that the good year was known by revelation, by the expected end of drought, or by God’s customary expansion after hardship, and from Rashīd Riḍā’s view that its detailed abundance was additional revelation rather than an implication of the dream. Joseph’s explanation is not merely a forecast of seven prosperous years followed by seven barren ones. It primarily directs the king to take the measures necessary to avert famine: cultivate and store provisions during the first period. The dream itself represents the king’s responsibility toward his subjects: fat cows signify the abundant years, lean cows the years of scarcity, their consumption of the fat cows the use of reserves during famine, and the ears depict preserving provisions.

Joseph adds three matters to this basic interpretation. “Except a little that you eat” is a permission to consume a limited part of the grain that should otherwise remain in its ear. “All except a little which you preserve” identifies the portion that must remain for seed and provisions in the ensuing year; the imperfect yaʾkulu-hunna, “eating them,” indicates continuing consumption rather than total exhaustion. Finally, Joseph deduces from the recurring number seven that a year of fertility follows the seven hard years. In that year provision will come without the special cultivation, storage, and administrative exertion required previously, which may explain the shift to the third person: the people, rather than the addressees, will be granted relief and will press.

Thus the replacement of drought by fertility is indeed inferred from the dream, though no text proves that this year exceeds other fertile years in bounty. The omission of “seven” before the dry ears supports the view that the dream chiefly portrays practical precautions, not merely a numerical chronology of fruitful and barren years. The most suitable reading is consequently rainfall, the growth of pasture, and the milking of livestock, corresponding to the cows in the vision.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan holds that the narrative tersely implies that the messenger, apparently the cupbearer, conveyed Joseph’s interpretation to the king. Alarmed by the coming drought and impressed by Joseph’s wisdom, the king ordered him brought forth in order to speak with him. This was not a mere summons of a prisoner who would return to confinement, but a call for release and acquittal; Joseph could therefore demand justice. His insistence led to the later, fuller decree: “Bring him to me, I will make him my favorite.”

Joseph addresses the messenger with restraint, asking him to return to his master and inquire into “the affair of women who cut their hands.” He avoids disparaging the prince’s wife or alleging more against the women than was needed to vindicate him. “My Lord is indeed well aware of their stratagems” is his only negative description and may be understood as a complaint to God.

The contrast between “your master” and “My Lord” subtly establishes the truth and refutes the claim that, in (12:23), Joseph used “my Lord” for the prince. The “affair” is the grave matter that made the women cut their hands: their overpowering infatuation with Joseph. By requiring the king to consider this, Joseph brings out the enormity of the trial and of resisting their sustained advances, a steadfastness possible only through God’s protection from evil by manifest proof.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains khaṭb as a serious matter that occasions discussion, and ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq as the truth becoming manifest when what had been hidden is uncovered. The concise narrative implies that, after the messenger returned and relayed Joseph’s demand, the king summoned and questioned the women about their attempt to solicit him.

They answer, “Heaven be praised! We know of no evil in him,” testifying that they found no fault in Joseph despite having sought to seduce him. Their exclamation, hāsha lillāh, parallels their earlier astonishment at his beauty and here indicates the utmost integrity and chastity that they knew in him.

The prince’s wife, the original cause of the trial, then confesses that she solicited Joseph and declares that he is truthful. Her statement assigns the attempted seduction wholly to herself and exonerates him from responding to, complying with, or inclining toward her. Together with the women’s emphatic testimony, her confession and attestation establish his complete innocence.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan holds that this unintroduced speech belongs to Joseph, as the Qurʾan often quotes words without expressly inserting “he said.” “This” refers to his sending the messenger back and demanding an inquiry; “he” and “him” refer to Potiphar, not the king. Joseph sought a judgment so that Potiphar would know that Joseph had not betrayed him in his absence by seeking his wife.

Joseph’s second purpose was to proclaim the divine principle that treachery cannot attain its end. Betrayal is falsehood, and falsehood is transient: God does not guide the treacherous, and their schemes must ultimately be exposed, as those of the women and Potiphar’s wife were. By conveying this principle to the king, Joseph also establishes that he can be entrusted with persons, missions, wealth, and secrets, preparing the way for his request to administer the country’s granaries.

The commentary further states that the king is distinct from Potiphar (al-ʿAzīz), the husband of the woman. Although some commentators assign this verse and the next to Potiphar’s wife, Al-Mizan treats that alternative below.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan regards this as the completion of Joseph’s speech. Having said that he did not betray Potiphar, Joseph immediately disavows any self-righteousness or inherent power. As a devoted monotheist, he attributes every good in himself, including his avoidance of betrayal, to his Lord’s mercy. The soul naturally urges human beings toward desires and evil; no one can claim immunity from this inclination except through God’s mercy, which turns the soul from wrongdoing toward righteous action.

The exception, “except inasmuch as my Lord has mercy,” both limits the universal tendency of the soul to evil and shows that good actions arising from divine mercy are also a natural inclination of the soul, not externally imposed compulsion. It specifically explains Joseph’s preservation from betrayal. By calling God “all-forgiving, all-merciful,” Joseph links forgiveness, which conceals faults and removes sins and their effects, with mercy, which brings forth goodness. Forgiveness therefore concerns deficiencies generally, not sins alone.

His repeated “my Lord” in this verse and (12:50) expresses his exclusive devotion to God and the special divine favor shown to him, whereas his use of “Allah” in saying that Allah does not further the schemes of the treacherous dissociates that general principle from himself.

Al-Mizan rejects the view that the relevant verses continue the prince’s wife’s speech. If “This, that he may know that I did not betray him” were hers and referred to her confession, it would be redundant and empty: she would be confessing merely to say that she had confessed. If it referred to her conduct while Joseph was imprisoned, it would conflict with the betrayal involved in entrapping and imprisoning him, and her confession could not establish complete loyalty. It would also be pointless for her to tell Joseph that Allah does not further treacherous schemes, a principle he had already invoked. Her admission that she does not absolve herself contradicts the alleged claim that she did not betray him, while the verse’s profound monotheistic knowledge is unlikely to be the speech of an idol-worshipping woman overcome by desire.

The alternative that she spoke to assure Potiphar that she had not physically betrayed him is also rejected. Her admission that she solicited Joseph, together with her testimony that he resisted, weighs against rather than reassures her, and cannot give Potiphar certainty about what occurred in private. Her later refusal to absolve herself would in any case be redundant after her earlier confession. The apparent sequence of the narrative instead supports Joseph as the speaker.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan explains astakhliṣ-hu as making Joseph exclusively attached to the king, and makīn as a person of rank and established status. The phrase “when he had spoken with him” omits the understood event that Joseph was brought before the king and conversed with him.

The restriction to “today” indicates why the king confers this position: Joseph’s avoidance of evil, illicit desire, betrayal, and oppression; his patience under trial in preserving purity; and his understanding, wisdom, and sound judgment. Since “honored and trustworthy” is unqualified, the decree is general: Joseph is given exceptional standing and trust with the king, authority over what he seeks, and responsibility in royal affairs.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains that, after the king granted Joseph unqualified honor and trust, Joseph asked to administer Egypt’s treasuries. He did so not for personal gain, but to oversee the collection and storage of provisions before the coming seven years of famine, then distribute them justly among the people.

His description of himself as ḥafīẓ, “fastidious,” and ʿalīm, “well-informed,” states the two qualities required for this responsibility. The ensuing context shows that the king granted him the office he requested.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan explains that makkannā means that God established Joseph in power, while yatabawwaʾu means that he could occupy or settle wherever he wished. “That is how” encompasses the preceding events through which Joseph reached authority in Egypt. His brothers’ envy, the well and slavery, the women’s attempts to compel him to immorality, and even the threat and reality of imprisonment were all turned by God into stages of his honor and rise.

His freedom to settle wherever he wished specifically contrasts with the confinement and loss of social freedom of prison. The verse also parallels the earlier establishment of Joseph in Potiphar’s house: “Thus We established Joseph in the land and that We might teach him the interpretation of dreams. Allah has command of His affairs (12:21).” As nothing could obstruct God’s mercy toward Joseph despite the apparent forces against him, nothing can prevent God’s decree when He wills mercy for someone.

“We do not waste the reward of the virtuous” refers to the power and reward bestowed on Joseph and promises all virtuous people that God will not let their deeds be lost.
verses.57: Al-Mizan holds that the promised reward of the Hereafter concerns God’s chosen servants, His awliyāʾ, among whom Joseph certainly belongs. It is not a promise to every believer without distinction: “those who have faith and are Godwary” denotes faith inseparably joined to constant, genuine piety. Such piety in turn cannot exist without faith; together they constitute the deeper faith and God-consciousness that lead to God’s guardianship (wilāya).
verses.58:
Al-Mizan states that the verse deliberately gives only essentials, since the account concerns Joseph’s reunion with his maternal brother, the divine favour shared by them, and Joseph’s eventual recognition by the others, rather than every event after his rise to power in Egypt.

The visiting group excluded this maternal brother, whom Jacob had kept apart from them after what had happened to Joseph, owing to his deep attachment to him. The brothers came only during the regional famine, after the seven abundant years and more than seven years after Joseph’s appointment over the granaries. They had not seen him since selling him to the caravan after taking him from the well as a boy; years in Potiphar’s house, prison, and administration of the granaries had elapsed. Appearing as an Egyptian official, and not suspected of being a Hebrew, Joseph was unrecognizable to them. Yet he recognized them immediately, either by his own sagacity or, possibly, prophetic insight.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that jahhaza-hum bi-jihāza-hum means that, after supplying them with the food they had bought, Joseph told them to bring the brother they had through their father. As al-Rāghib states, jihāz denotes supplies, while tajhīz means carrying or sending them.

Joseph’s appeal, “Do you not see that I give the full measure,” means that he neither gives short measure nor wrongs them by abusing his power; “I am the best of hosts” means that he is most generous in hospitality and lodging. These words encouraged their return with the brother, while the ensuing warning that they would receive no rations and must not approach him if they failed to bring him was intended to secure their obedience. Their later promise to solicit him from his father accepted this requirement and reassured Joseph.

The commentary holds that Joseph’s emphatic request, inducement, and threat must have followed some preliminary exchange that did not disclose that he was Joseph or arouse their suspicions. It rejects the many detailed dialogues invented by commentators as unsupported by the Qurʾanic account or its context. At most, it may be inferred that Joseph asked about their circumstances; the ten brothers told him of another brother who remained with a father unable to bear separation from him for travel or otherwise, and this led the governor Joseph to ask that he be brought so that he might see him.
verses.60: Al-Mizan explains that kayl, “rations,” is the measured provision. Joseph warns that, unless they bring their brother, they will receive no provisions from him and will neither approach him nor be permitted to enter his land or appear before him to buy food.
verses.61: Al-Mizan explains that murāwada in sa-nurāwid ʿan-hu abā-hu denotes persistently returning to a matter and earnestly pleading for it. The brothers’ promise to persuade “his father” indicates that they had told Joseph how deeply their father loved this brother and could not bear his absence for travel or otherwise; saying “his father,” rather than “our father,” reinforces this. “We will surely do” commits them either to bringing the brother or to persuading their father to let him travel with them to meet Joseph, thereby reassuring him and giving guarantees.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains that fityān means young boys or attendants, and that biḍāʿa, though used in several senses, here means the commodities the brothers had brought to Egypt to trade for food. Riḥāl are containers or baggage for goods, while inqalabū means returning home.

Joseph ordered his attendants to return the brothers’ payment to their saddlebags. Perhaps, upon returning to their people and opening the bags, they would recognize their goods and come back; the kindness might win their hearts and lead them to expect further generosity.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains iktiyāl, from which naktal is derived, as obtaining food by measure. The brothers tell their father that they will receive no grain unless their brother accompanies them to Egypt; they therefore ask to take him so that they may obtain provisions and avoid deprivation. Calling him “our brother” and promising to protect him are meant to express tenderness and reassure their father of their commitment.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains Jacob’s question as a reminder that he had once trusted these sons with Joseph, accepted their assurance that they would protect him, and was then met with their false account of Joseph’s death. Their assurance concerning Benjamin consequently provides no real security.

Jacob’s declaration that Allah is the best protector does not mean that entrusting a matter to people is, in itself, shirk; prophets are remote from such association, and Jacob himself had previously entrusted Joseph to his sons. Rather, God is preferable to every human protector because His perfect mercy and attributes ensure that He does not fail one who relies on Him, whereas people may betray a trust, fail to show mercy, and lack independent power and will.

This also explains why Jacob later demands a pledge by Allah while excepting circumstances in which they are made powerless: the pledge concerns harms or abandonment within their control, not unavoidable events. “He is the most merciful of merciful ones” subtly recalls that they showed little, or perhaps no, mercy toward Joseph despite promising to protect him.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains that the brothers’ recovered capital proves the Egyptian governor returned both their payment and their provisions. Their rhetorical “what do we want?” expresses astonishment at his generosity and is intended to reassure their father that the journey was beneficial and that the governor meant them no harm. They use this to urge him to send their brother: they will provision their family, protect him, and obtain an additional camel-load, which they regard as easy.

The commentary records alternative readings: mā in mā nabghī may be negative, meaning that they do not seek to deceive their father about the governor’s generosity; and yasīr may mean a small measure, so that their present provisions are insufficient and they need their brother’s additional share.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains mawthiqan min Allāh as a reliable pledge made under divine authority, such as an oath or covenant invoking God. One who swears thus places God’s sanctity behind his undertaking and is answerable to God if he breaks it. The exception illā an yuḥāṭ bi-kum means that the sons are excused only if calamity overwhelms them, leaves them powerless, and prevents Benjamin’s return.

Allah as wakīl is the One entrusted with and directing affairs. Reliance on God does not deny actions, causes, or ordinary means; it denies that persons and means possess independent power, while affirming God as the sole independent director. Jacob accordingly employs ordinary means—speaking to his sons and taking their pledge—then relies upon God, as he will again do when directing them to enter by separate gates.

Thus Jacob will not release Benjamin until they swear to bring him back insofar as it lies within their power. Once they pledge, his words, “Allah is a trustee over what we say,” place both their undertaking and the means they have adopted under God’s guardianship: He ensures fulfillment and recompenses breach of trust.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan explains that Jacob orders all eleven sons to enter Egypt through separate gates because he fears that public attention might expose their united group to the evil eye, envy, fear, violence, or another calamity that would scatter or reduce them. The context appears to suggest a divine intuition that their impressive unity would soon be broken, so he adopts this precaution in hope of averting it.

Yet he immediately states that it cannot avail them against Allah, for sovereignty and judgment belong only to Him. Visible precautions have no independent effect and operate only by God’s will. Jacob’s reliance on God therefore accompanies, rather than abandons, the means He has established.

The verse defines tawakkul as entrusting one’s affair to another. Since ordinary means are dependent and insufficient by themselves, a person seeking vital ends must both use them and rely on the cause beyond them that enables them. Neglecting means is ignorance, but reliance is due exclusively to God, without partner, as “in Him let all the trusting put their trust” indicates.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan understands the brothers’ entering as their father commanded to mean entering Egypt, or the governor’s residence, through separate gates. Jacob had used this precaution to avert a foreseen scattering or reduction of his sons, but it could not repel God’s decree: Benjamin was retained on account of the cup, and the eldest brother remained in Egypt.

Nevertheless, this same course fulfilled Jacob’s personal wish, his continuing longing for Joseph. Benjamin’s retention and the brothers’ later return to Joseph led eventually to Joseph’s disclosure and the reunion of Jacob and his family. The exception in “but only fulfilled a wish in Jacob’s heart” may mean simply that God would fulfill Jacob’s longing; more plausibly, it is a genuine exception: the precaution benefited neither Jacob nor his sons generally, except that God fulfilled this particular desire.

“Indeed he had the knowledge of what We had taught him” praises Jacob for divinely bestowed, rather than conventionally acquired, knowledge. Such knowledge does not err; it validates his anticipation of trial, his use of available means, his reliance on God, and his enduring longing for Joseph.

The commentary reports other interpretations: some say the advice merely eased Jacob’s anxiety although it could not avert a decreed evil eye or other harm; others say an ordained evil eye would have reached the brothers whether they travelled together or separately. Some interpret the divine teaching as Jacob’s certainty and knowledge of God, unrecognized by most people, or take the lām in wa inna-hu la-dhū ʿilmin limā ʿallamnā-hu as emphasizing that Jacob acted upon what God taught him.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph drew Benjamin, his full brother, close to himself and secretly disclosed, “Indeed I am your brother”: he was Joseph, whom Benjamin had lost. He consoles him over the mistreatment and jealousy of their other brothers, or perhaps over their intended plan to leave Benjamin with Joseph.

The commentary rejects the claim that Joseph merely meant he would replace a deceased maternal brother. The emphatic wording better indicates disclosure of his identity, and Joseph’s later statement, “I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Certainly Allah has shown us favor,” presupposes that Benjamin already knew who he was.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains saqāya as a drinking vessel, raḥl as a camel saddle, and ʿīr as a travelling group and its goods-bearing camels. Joseph’s placing the cup in his brother’s saddle was a plan to keep him with Joseph, preparing for the later disclosure of Joseph’s identity and their divine favor.

The herald’s charge addresses the entire caravan although the cup would be found only among one member’s belongings; until a search identified him, such collective address was justified. The context indicates that Joseph’s full brother knew and expected the plan: he neither defended himself nor showed distress. The charge was therefore not a genuine accusation from Joseph’s perspective but a formal designation used to retain him. It was not a forbidden baseless accusation, since the announcing herald presumably did not know the reality.

Some exegetes say the herald was one of Joseph’s people who had genuinely lost the measuring cup and did not know Joseph had ordered it placed in his brother’s saddle. Abū Muslim interprets the proclamation as Joseph’s allusion to the brothers’ having “stolen” Joseph from his father and cast him into the well. Others construe it as an omitted interrogative, “Are you indeed thieves?”; the commentary considers this unlikely.
verses.71: Al-Mizan explains faqd as the loss of an object from one’s awareness so that its whereabouts are unknown. The brothers, called the caravan, turn back toward Joseph and his attendants and ask what they are missing. The context indicates that the herald called after them once they had begun their journey.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains that the suwāʿ is the saqāya of the preceding verse: a king’s vessel used for drinking and, apparently, measuring, which accounts for its being called both a drinking vessel and a measuring bowl and for masculine and feminine pronouns being used of it. A ḥaml is a load, and zaʿīm means guarantor or warrantor, and may also mean a leader.

The commentary considers it possible that one of Joseph’s servants says that the king’s goblet is missing, while Joseph himself guarantees a camel-load to whoever brings it, since he is the authority who grants and guarantees rewards. Some interpreters instead take the reward statement as continuing the herald’s earlier proclamation, with the intervening exchange treated as parenthetical.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains that “this country” is Egypt. The brothers’ assertion that Joseph’s people know they came not to cause trouble implies that, on their first arrival, they had been thoroughly questioned at Joseph’s command as possible spies or men with malicious intentions—about their purpose, origin, lineage, and family. This supports reports that Joseph feigned suspicion and thereby learned of their aged father and brother.

Their denial that they are thieves repudiates not only the present charge but the possession of such a vile trait by themselves or their family.
verses.74: Al-Mizan explains that Joseph’s servants, or Joseph together with them, ask what the penalty for theft should be if the brothers’ denial is false. Calling them liars has the same force as the preceding accusation that they are thieves.
verses.75: Al-Mizan explains that, under Jacob’s law, the penalty for theft was that the thief himself became the servant of the person whose property he stole. By saying that the requital is the person in whose saddlebag the item is found, the brothers stress that only the individual thief—not his companions—should be punished, and that the owner of the stolen property may take him and determine his fate.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph searches the other brothers’ sacks before Benjamin’s in order to conceal his intention and prevent suspicion that he had placed the cup in Benjamin’s sack. Once it is found there, the consequence prescribed by the brothers themselves follows.

“Thus did We devise for Joseph’s sake” attributes the strategy to God’s inspiration or revelation. It enabled Joseph to separate his full brother from the others without their consent, which they would have withheld had they known his purpose. Although all planning falls under God’s domain, His purity is above schemes involving oppression, betrayal, or evil intent.

Joseph could not have kept Benjamin under the Egyptian king’s law, which did not enslave a thief. By God’s guidance, he arranged the accusation so that the brothers, after denying it, would state their own law that the thief be enslaved; Joseph then retained Benjamin by the standard they had accepted. The passage indicates that a criminal could be subjected to the punishment his own law prescribed, even when it was severe.

God’s raising whom He wills in rank manifests His favor in elevating Joseph above his brothers. “Above every man of knowledge is One who knows best” shows that acquired knowledge, denoted by dhī ʿilm, admits of one more knowledgeable above it. God’s limitless, essential knowledge is not such an acquired possession and is beyond spatial hierarchy, limit, or definition. It is plausible that the indefinite ʿalīm refers to God Himself, emphasizing His incomparable and indefinable knowledge.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph’s half-brothers distance themselves from Benjamin’s alleged theft by claiming that Joseph, his full brother, had stolen before and that the two shared this trait through their maternal lineage. Yet this contradicts their earlier collective denial, “and we are not thieves” (12:73), and exposes their enduring envy of Joseph and Benjamin.

Joseph conceals the truth concerning their allegation: he neither defends himself nor discloses the reality. His inward judgment, “You are in a worse state! And Allah knows best what you allege,” alludes to their contradiction, envy, and audacity to lie before the governor despite his benevolence.

Some commentators take “You are in a worse state” to mean that they had committed a worse act by taking Joseph from his father, while God knows whether Joseph had ever stolen. The commentary considers this possible in implication but unsuitable to the context in which Joseph conceals his identity. It also rejects the view that Joseph concealed only the words “You are in a worse state” and openly uttered merely “Allah knows best what you allege.”
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains that, once the brothers realize Benjamin is liable to detention and enslavement, they remember their oath to return him safely and cannot face their father without him. They therefore plead with the governor to take any one of them instead, so Benjamin may return to his very old father. Their appeal is framed to stir the governor’s chivalry and kindness.
verses.79: Al-Mizan explains this as Joseph’s refusal of his brothers’ proposal that one of them be taken instead of Benjamin: to take anyone other than the person in whose possession the wares were found would be wrongdoing.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains istayʾasū as losing all hope and khalaṣū najiyyan as withdrawing for private consultation. The brothers despair of Joseph—though the pronoun could refer to Benjamin—releasing their brother even in exchange for one of themselves, and privately consider whether to return without him or remain.

Their eldest recalls their father’s pledge by Allah to bring Benjamin back and their earlier failure regarding Joseph: they had promised to protect him, then cast him into a well, sold him to a caravan, and told their father a wolf had eaten him. He resolves not to leave Egypt until his father permits it or Allah judges for him. This means he awaits a way out of an apparently closed situation, perhaps Benjamin’s unforeseen release, his own death, or another unanticipated solution, while directing the others to return to their father.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan takes “we testified only to what we knew” most fittingly to mean that the brothers testify only to Benjamin’s apparent theft. Another interpretation makes it their testimony before the ruler that a thief should be liable under their law, but this fits the context less well.

“We could not have forestalled the unseen” means that they did not know Benjamin was a thief or would steal the drinking vessel and be apprehended. Had they known, they would neither have taken him nor made their oath concerning him; their testimony about the penalty rested only on what they knew.
verses.82: Al-Mizan explains that the brothers invite Jacob to ask the people of the Egyptian city and the caravan that travelled with them and witnessed their dealings with the ruler. They offer these witnesses to remove doubt that they were negligent and to confirm Benjamin’s alleged theft, reinforcing their claim that they speak the truth.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan explains that the omitted details in the preceding verses indicate that Jacob said this after his sons conveyed the account instructed by their eldest brother. Jacob did not deny an account supported by evident signs and verifiable witnesses, nor accuse his sons of deliberate ill intent. Rather, through divinely inspired insight, he discerned that the new incident was an offshoot of the self-deception that had produced the earlier affair of Joseph.

“Maybe Allah will bring them all to me” includes Joseph, his brother, and the eldest brother who remained behind in Egypt. Jacob therefore regards the loss of the two latter sons, like Joseph’s earlier loss, as something his sons had brought upon themselves; he responds with graceful patience and hopes for the return of all three. This refutes the view that he simply judged their account false and thought they had invented a different story.

His words are an expression of hope, not merely a supplication, and imply that he believes Joseph remains alive. His appeal to Allah as “the All-knowing, the All-wise” rests on confidence that God knows the conditions of election and the completion of His favor, and wisely directs affairs. Jacob thus hopes that God will restore his sons and complete His favor to his family; trials should not lead one to impulsiveness, despair, or loss of hope in God’s mercy. These are the same two divine attributes Jacob had previously mentioned to Joseph and which Joseph later recalled at the fulfillment of his dream.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains, citing al-Rāghib, that asaf may denote grief or anger: the heart’s boiling desire for requital appears as anger toward one beneath oneself and as sorrow toward one above oneself. Kaẓīm denotes holding back one’s breath and thereby suppressing what would otherwise escape; it can signify silence and the restraint of anger.

Jacob turned away after addressing his sons, cried, “Alas for Joseph (yā asfā ʿalā Yūsuf)!,” and lost his sight from grief. Although eyes “turning white” can sometimes suggest partial sight, Joseph’s later statement that his shirt would restore Jacob’s sight shows that it here means complete blindness. Jacob nevertheless suppressed his anger and swallowed his sorrow, without confronting his sons.
verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains that ḥaraḍ and ḥāriḍ mean being close to death. Though some interpret ḥaraḍ as a state in which one is neither dead enough to forget misery nor alive enough to hope for relief, the former meaning is stronger because it is paired with al-hālikīn, those who perish. The singular form ḥaraḍ is a verbal noun and therefore is not pluralized like hālikīn.

The brothers thus say that Jacob has remembered and mentioned Joseph without cease for years and will continue until he is near death or dies. Apparently they speak from sympathy and concern for his condition, though it is possible that frustration at his continual weeping and prolonged mourning also motivates them, particularly because his grief and denunciation of them implied blame for Joseph’s affair.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī, explains baththī as a profound distress that cannot be contained and so is spread or disclosed. The restrictive wording, “I complain of my anguish and grief only to Allah,” means that Jacob does not complain to his sons or household; he directs his sorrow exclusively to God, who is never wearied by His servants’ petitions.

Jacob’s statement, “I know from Allah what you do not know,” is therefore the ground of his refusal to despair of God’s solace or lose hope in His mercy. It gives a general indication of his knowledge of God whose particular scope is understood from the context.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī, explains taḥassasū as seeking something by the senses, akin to tajassus. Views differ on their distinction: some regard them as effectively synonymous; others say tajassus searches for people’s faults while taḥassus eavesdrops; and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that taḥassus concerns good and tajassus evil.

Rawḥ Allāh, rendered here as Allah’s mercy, literally suggests breath or a pleasant breath and figuratively denotes the comfort and expansiveness of relief after suffocating hardship. Jacob commands his sons to seek Joseph and his brother in Egypt and not despair of the relief God may grant. Since God does as He wills and none can overturn His decree, despair of His mercy amounts to denying His power and all-encompassing mercy; it belongs to the faithless. According to the traditions, despair of God’s mercy is among the gravest sins.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains that biḍāʿa muzjāt means a small amount of trading goods. Jacob’s sons came before Joseph, whose identity they still did not know, with two pressing requests that seemed unlikely to succeed. They needed food although their capital was inadequate, and their earlier allegations of deception and theft had damaged their standing with the official. They also sought their detained brother, but, after their previous request to substitute another brother had been refused, they did not ask directly for his release.

They therefore spoke with extreme humility: they described the hardship afflicting their family, acknowledged their meager capital, asked for the full measure of provisions, and appealed for charity. Their request for charity encompasses both food and their brother’s release, since he was in effect the official’s property; “Indeed Allah rewards the charitable” also functions as an implicit prayer. Thus, Joseph’s brothers sought mercy from the powerful official despite their circumstances and prior dealings with him.

At this point God’s decree to elevate Joseph and his brother and humble the other sons because of their wrongdoing was realized. Joseph revealed himself only when they stood powerless and humbled before him, while the brother whom they had envied was honored beside him; though he could have informed his father and brothers earlier, God willed this confrontation from a position of power.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph’s question, “Have you realized what you did to Joseph and his brother,” is a rhetorical reminder to wrongdoers of the consequences of what they know they did. By adding, “when you were senseless,” he implicitly excuses them.

He does not rebuke them or call them to account; rather, he reminds them of their deed so that they may recognize God’s extraordinary kindness to Joseph and his brother. This manifests Joseph’s exceptional magnanimity and nobility.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains that the brothers’ emphatic question, “Are you really Joseph?!,” follows from conclusive evidence that the Egyptian governor was the brother whom they had thrown into the well and sold into slavery; it seeks acknowledgment rather than proof. Joseph answers, “I am Joseph, and this is my brother,” mentioning his brother, though they had not asked about him, to show that Allah had favored them both, the two whom the brothers had envied.

Joseph then attributes this favor to Godwariness and patience: Allah does not waste the reward of the virtuous. In doing so, he calls his brothers to righteousness and shows that it is attained through piety and patience.
verses.91: Al-Mizan explains that īthār means choosing and giving preference, while khaṭaʾ is the opposite of correctness and khātiʾ denotes one who is in error. The brothers thus acknowledge that Allah has preferred Joseph over them and confess their own wrongdoing.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains tathrīb as excessive blame, reproach, and recounting of sins. Joseph’s declaration that there shall be no reproach “today” signifies a special act of forgiveness: he overlooks any desire for revenge while he stands as Egypt’s mighty governor, endowed with prophecy and knowledge, beside his brother, and they stand humbled, confessing their error and Allah’s preference for him. This reverses their earlier attitude toward Joseph and his brother.

Joseph then prays, “May Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.” His plea seeks forgiveness for all his brothers who collectively wronged him, not only those then present; the passage infers that not all were present from the subsequent verse, They said, ‘By God, you persist in your inveterate error’ (12:95).
verses.93:
Al-Mizan explains that Joseph tells his brothers to lay his shirt upon Jacob’s face so that God may restore the sight Jacob lost through grief and weeping over Joseph. This is the final miraculous intervention in Joseph’s favor in the chapter: God repeatedly turned the brothers’ envy, their casting him into the well, his sale into slavery, the women’s attempted seduction, and his imprisonment into means of his innocence, honor, and authority.

The blood-stained shirt the brothers had once used to support their false claim of Joseph’s death had caused Jacob’s blinding grief; Joseph’s shirt now becomes the means by which God restores his sight. Thus, apparent causes of Joseph’s ruin were made instruments of his elevation, for God’s will prevails over appearances. Joseph’s command to bring “all your folks” orders the entire house of Jacob—Jacob, his family, children, and descendants—to leave their pastoral life and settle in Egypt.
verses.94: Al-Mizan explains that faṣalat al-ʿīr means that the caravan separated or departed, while tufannidūni derives from fand, poor judgment or lack of wisdom. When the caravan carrying Joseph’s shirt had left Egypt and was far away, Jacob sensed Joseph’s familiar scent, anticipating their reunion. His sons’ earlier accusations that he was deluded made him qualify this perception by asking that they not judge him a dotard.
verses.95:
Al-Mizan explains that Jacob’s sons repeat at the story’s end the same charge they made at its beginning: their father persists in his old, or long-standing, ḍalāl. They meant not religious deviation, which would amount to unbelief, but what they regarded as his misplaced preferential love for Joseph and Benjamin.

Seeing themselves as numerous, strong, and responsible for the household’s protection, the elder sons thought themselves more deserving of Jacob’s affection than his two youngest sons, whom they considered to offer no comparable support. Jacob’s continuing grief for Joseph—until he lost his sight and became bent-backed—deepened their frustration. Their statements elsewhere show that they were monotheists following the religion of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and nothing in either occurrence of ḍalāl indicates a religious error; it concerns a practical, personal judgment about paternal favoritism.
verses.96: Al-Mizan identifies the bearer of good news as the man who brought Joseph’s shirt to Jacob. Once it was placed upon Jacob’s face and his sight returned, Jacob reminded his sons of his earlier reply when they reproached him for remembering Joseph: “I complain of my anguish and grief only to Allah. I know from Allah what you do not know.”
verses.97: Al-Mizan explains that the speakers are Jacob’s sons, as their address to “our father” shows. Their request for forgiveness concerns their sins against Joseph and his brother; Joseph himself had already prayed for their forgiveness.
verses.98: Al-Mizan notes that Jacob postpones seeking forgiveness for his sons, since sawfa in sawfa astaghfiru la-kum indicates future action. Perhaps he delayed until he could fully enjoy reunion with Joseph and his heart could recover from the pain of separation. Traditions also suggest that he deferred the supplication to a time when prayers are more likely to be answered.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan states that the verse leaves the family’s migration from their land to Egypt implicit. On their arrival, Joseph “set his parents close to himself,” understood as embracing them. His welcome to Egypt suggests that he had gone out to receive them and then invited them into the city as an act of honor.

By assuring them entry “in safety, God willing,” Joseph speaks with the authority of a ruler who can grant security and authorize their settlement, yet makes that authority contingent on God’s will. This expresses pure monotheism: human intentions take effect only when they accord with the divine will. Although commentators dispute whether “his parents” means Joseph’s biological mother and father or Jacob and his maternal aunt, the Qurʾanic wording supplies no evidence decisively supporting either view; its apparent sense is his actual parents. The verse thus concerns the arrival of Joseph’s parents, brothers, and their households before him outside Egypt, his embrace of his parents, and his assurance of their safe entry.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains that the ʿarsh is an elevated royal dais, kharūr means falling to the ground, and badw denotes the Bedouin desert life from which Jacob’s family came. Joseph seated his parents on the royal throne in honor, apparently by the agency of his attendants. Their prostration likely occurred when they saw Joseph.

The pronoun in “they fell down prostrate before him” refers to Joseph, not God; there is no linguistic evidence for the contrary interpretation. Yet this was not worship of Joseph. Jacob and Joseph were both devoted to God alone and free from associating partners with Him. The family therefore took Joseph as a divine sign and as the direction of their prostration, while worshipping God, just as the Kaʿba provides a direction for prayer without being its object. On this reading, claims that it was merely an ordinary greeting, a permitted social custom, or simply a kind of bowing lack textual support.

When Joseph saw his parents and eleven brothers prostrate, he recognized the realization of the childhood dream in which eleven stars, the sun, and moon prostrated to him. He thanked God for bringing him out of prison and granting him honor and leadership. Delicately, and in the presence of his brothers, he did not mention the well or explicitly blame them; he attributed the division between them to Satan’s incitement and described God as having brought the family from the desert to Egypt.

His words present his ordeals—especially separation from his father and imprisonment—as immense hardships that God turned, one after another, from causes of humiliation and destruction into comfort, life, honor, and authority. This is why he calls God laṭīf in bringing about what He wills: God’s subtle, attentive care reaches even the most remote and intricate circumstances and transforms them by His encompassing knowledge and power. The closing names, the All-knowing and the All-wise, explain the fulfillment of the dream and the whole course of divine favor; they also correspond to Jacob’s earlier description of God and may emphatically affirm its truth.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan explains that, after recounting God’s favors, Joseph turns from addressing his father to addressing God alone: God granted him a share in kingship and taught him the interpretation of dreams. By calling Him the Originator of the heavens and earth and his guardian in this world and the Hereafter, Joseph returns to the principle of divine guardianship, wilāya, already manifested in his release from prison, his family’s arrival from the desert, his kingdom, and his knowledge.

Divine wilāya is God’s sustaining of every being in its essence, attributes, and actions. It follows from His bringing all things from nonexistence into manifest existence; hence He is the Originator of the heavens and earth. Joseph, as one sincerely devoted to God, thereby acknowledges that he has no independent agency, attributes, actions, benefit, harm, life, death, or resurrection, but is wholly under God’s guardianship.

His request, “Let my death be in submission, and unite me with the Righteous,” asks for submission throughout his worldly life and for companionship with the righteous in the Hereafter. The perfection of divine servanthood is total surrender: obeying what God wants, avoiding what He dislikes, and claiming none of one’s achievements as independent of Him. It is also to be righteous and worthy of nearness to God and His blessings in matters beyond the servant’s choice. This is the highest degree of submission and servanthood, comparable to what was granted to Abraham.

Accordingly, tawafianī musliman does not ask God to cause Joseph’s death, nor merely ask that he happen to die as a Muslim after an otherwise unsubmissive life. It asks God to preserve Joseph’s sincerity and submission continuously until God takes him. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the early exegetical claim that Joseph was requesting death.
verses.102: Al-Mizan explains that “these” refers to the story of Joseph, while the address is to the Prophet Muḥammad. “They” and “them” refer to Joseph’s brothers, and ajmaʿū, derived from ijmāʿ, signifies their collective resolve and intention to act. The clause that the Prophet was not with them when they conspired and schemed qualifies the revelation itself: the story is an account of the Unseen because it is revealed to one who was not present when Joseph’s brothers determined upon their plot against him.
verses.103: Al-Mizan explains that most people will not believe, however earnestly the Prophet desires it, because they are deeply attached to worldly life and its attractions and neglect the innate knowledge of God and His signs placed within their nature. The following verses furnish the evidence for this claim.
verses.104: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet asks no payment for either people’s faith or the Qurʾan he recites to them; hence the cost of giving up their wealth is not what prevents their acceptance. The Qurʾan is solely a reminder for all humanity, recalling the knowledge of God and His signs that He has implanted in their hearts but that heedlessness has made them forget. It is not a means of gaining wealth, honor, prestige, or anything else.
verses.105: Al-Mizan notes that the initial waw may be adverbial, “While how many a sign there is…,” or begin a new discourse. Murūr, from which yamurrūn ʿalay-hā derives, is to encounter something and move past it; here it means repeatedly witnessing the signs in heaven and earth. Their existence and exquisite order indicate their Creator’s oneness, yet people turn away from them heedlessly. If “they pass by” is understood literally, the verse also supports modern astronomy’s account of the Earth’s rotation and orbit: inhabitants of Earth pass celestial bodies despite sensory appearances.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan explains that, despite the absence of any demanded reward and the abundance of signs of God’s oneness, most people do not truly believe; and among the minority who do believe, most mix faith with some form of polytheism.

Though faith in the One God and associating partners with Him are opposites, they may coexist in varying degrees and relations. Faith is the heart’s attachment and submission to God’s ultimate reality, whereas polytheism is attachment to other entities that possess no power except by His permission. At one extreme, one may be absorbed in fleeting worldly allurements and forget all truth; at the other, God’s devoted servants detach themselves from distractions, remember and rely upon Him alone, and desire only what He desires. Between these extremes are degrees in which faith and polytheism coexist.

This is evident when one professes belief yet fears every threatened calamity, seeks honor from others despite “All honor belongs to Allah (10:65),” pursues provision through every door although God has guaranteed it, or disobeys Him without shame despite believing that He knows, hears, and sees all. The verse thus concerns forms of polytheism compatible with degrees of faith, called ‘hidden polytheism’ (al-shirk al-khafī). It is therefore unwarranted to restrict its polytheists solely to Meccan idol-worshippers or to the hypocrites (munāfiqūn).
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains ghāshiya as an enveloping divine punishment and baghtatan as its suddenness. “While they are unaware” describes people being overtaken by the Hour without signs disclosing its exact time or onset. The rhetorical question expresses astonishment that those heedless of the heavenly and earthly signs, lacking pure faith and absorbed in worldly heedlessness, should feel secure from an encompassing punishment or from the Hour’s sudden arrival.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan explains that God commands the Prophet to declare his path: summoning people to the pure monotheism demonstrated by the signs in heaven and earth, with clear understanding and insight. “This is my way” declares that approach; “I summon to Allah with insight” defines it; “Immaculate is Allah” affirms His utter transcendence; and “I am not one of the polytheists” shows that the call is founded on monotheism untainted by association.

“I and he who follows me” extends the responsibility of this call beyond the Prophet to his true followers. Yet the context limits this participation: the way in question is calling to pure faith and real monotheism with insight and certainty, and only those sincerely devoted to God, aware of their Lord’s stature, and possessing such insight can share it. It does not include everyone who merely claims to follow the Prophet, especially those characterized by polytheism, heedlessness of God, security from His punishment, and turning away from His signs. Such people are described elsewhere as misguided, blind, and lost, qualities incompatible with true guidance or calling others to God.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet’s preaching is not novel but follows the established divine way: earlier messengers were revealed to men from the towns, not angels, who lived among and were known to the people they called. Their being described as townsmen perhaps emphasizes this familiarity and that they were not outsiders; their description as men supports this, since men are more familiar than veiled women.

Travel through the land enables the Prophet’s community to see the ruins and deserted dwellings of earlier nations, which warn of the consequences of disbelief, denial, and rejecting God’s signs. Like the earlier prophets, the Prophet calls people only to what benefits them: Godwariness (taqwā), success in this world, and enduring happiness in the Hereafter. The Hereafter is better for the Godwary, and this is the essential message to which reason should lead them.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan distinguishes istayʾasa from complete yaʾs: although commonly treated as synonymous, istayʾasa denotes the approach or first signs of despair rather than utter despair. The verse completes the preceding account of the messengers’ mission: prophets, men from towns, called their peoples, who neither responded nor ceased despite warnings of punishment. When the messengers had lost hope that their peoples would believe them, and those peoples thought the messengers’ warnings of punishment were lies, God’s help came. He delivered whom He willed—the believers—and His might and punishment were not turned away from the guilty.

The commentary finds this reading borne out by the accounts of Noah and other prophets: Noah was told that no further members of his people would believe (11:36), while his people called him a liar (11:27). Other verses likewise describe God’s help for the faithful and His destruction of guilty nations, and affirm that when God wills ill for a people none can avert it (13:11). This interpretation best culminates the preceding verse’s message; the other proposed explanations have weaknesses and should be set aside.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan cites al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī that ʿibra and iʿtibār mean moving from witnessing an event to grasping its unseen implication. “Their accounts” refers to the prophets, including Joseph, though it may also refer to Joseph and his brothers. Their stories therefore provide a lesson for people of intellect.

The account in this sūrah is not fabricated, but confirms what preceded the Qurʾan—namely the Torah, Moses’ scripture, in which Joseph’s story is mentioned. Its “elaboration of all things” is a clear, discriminating explanation of all that people require for faith and for happiness in this world and the Hereafter. It is guidance to prosperity and success, and a special divine mercy guiding believers to the straight path.
